chapters.title: Introduction: Formulation of the problem
chapters.summary: Integrate the imaging with prior clinical observations and predicted physiology. The diagnostic approach synthesizes history, examination, ECG, radiography and advanced imaging into a coherent anatomic–physiologic explanation.

chapters.title: Functional murmurs
chapters.summary: A Still murmur. The typical Still murmur is vibratory or buzzing, midsystolic and most prominent between the apex and lower left sternal edge in the supine child.

chapters.title: The cardiac malpositions
chapters.summary: Secondary cardiac displacement. Cardiac displacement is a secondary shift in intrathoracic position, such as one produced by diaphragmatic eventration.

chapters.title: Isolated congenital complete heart block
chapters.summary: Transplacental transfer of maternal IgG with injury to fetal conduction tissue. The source describes passive autoimmunity involving maternal IgG antibodies, including Ro/SSA and La/SSB associations; maternal lupus can become apparent only later.

chapters.title: Congenital abnormalities of the pericardium
chapters.summary: Herniation of the left atrial appendage through a partial left pericardial defect. Partial absence of the left pericardium may permit left atrial appendage herniation, producing the described convex left-border shadow.

chapters.title: Congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries
chapters.summary: Atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial discordance. Two discordant junctions place systemic venous blood in the pulmonary circuit and pulmonary venous blood in the systemic circuit, so the circulations are in series.

chapters.title: Congenital aortic stenosis: Congenital aortic regurgitation
chapters.summary: A mobile stenotic aortic valve. The sound arises from abrupt movement of a mobile doming valve and identifies valvar level rather than degree.

chapters.title: Coarctation of the aorta and interrupted aortic arch
chapters.summary: Compare upper-extremity and femoral pulses and blood pressures. Upper–lower extremity pulse and pressure differences are hallmarks; brachial–femoral comparison is particularly practical in infants.

chapters.title: Congenital obstruction to left atrial flow: Mitral stenosis, cor triatriatum, pulmonary vein stenosis
chapters.summary: Parachute mitral valve. A single papillary muscle receiving all chordae defines the parachute arrangement and can restrict interchordal flow.

chapters.title: Congenital pulmonary stenosis and regurgitation
chapters.summary: Dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis. Dysplastic pulmonary stenosis has thickened separate poorly mobile leaflets without commissural fusion.

chapters.title: Ebstein’s anomaly of the tricuspid valve
chapters.summary: The inlet right ventricle between the anatomic annulus and displaced functional valve. Apical displacement atrializes the proximal inlet right ventricle while the trabecular and outlet portions form the functional right ventricle.

chapters.title: Atrial septal defect: Simple and complex
chapters.summary: Relative compliance of the two ventricles. With little atrial pressure difference, preferential filling of the more compliant right ventricle produces the usual left-to-right shunt.

chapters.title: Pulmonary stenosis with interatrial communication
chapters.summary: Patent foramen ovale. Severe pulmonary stenosis with right-to-left shunting most often uses a patent foramen ovale; a nonrestrictive secundum defect more often accompanies mild-to-moderate stenosis and left-to-right flow.

chapters.title: Ventricular septal defect
chapters.summary: Restrictive defect. Restriction at the defect limits pressure transmission and shunt flow, leaving a systolic pressure difference.

chapters.title: Ventricular septal defect with pulmonary stenosis
chapters.summary: Anterior and cephalad deviation of the infundibular septum. Outlet septal malalignment creates the ventricular defect, narrows right ventricular outflow and contributes to aortic override.

chapters.title: Double outlet ventricle
chapters.summary: Double outlet right ventricle. The chapter uses ventricular support of most of both arterial valves as its pragmatic definition while acknowledging classification debates.

chapters.title: Patent ductus arteriosus and aortopulmonary window
chapters.summary: Patent ductus arteriosus. The normal ductal insertion is near the left pulmonary artery, with its aortic end distal to the left subclavian artery.

chapters.title: Anomalous origin of the left coronary artery from the pulmonary trunk
chapters.summary: Falling pulmonary pressure reduces antegrade perfusion through the anomalous artery. Initially high pulmonary pressure can support antegrade flow. Its postnatal fall reduces that supply unless intercoronary perfusion becomes adequate.

chapters.title: Congenital coronary arterial fistula
chapters.summary: Congenital coronary arterial fistula. A fistulous branch provides an abnormal drainage route despite usually appropriate coronary origins.

chapters.title: Congenital aneurysms of the sinuses of valsalva
chapters.summary: Right atrium. The noncoronary sinus is anatomically related to the right atrium; right coronary sinus aneurysms commonly enter the right ventricle or sometimes the right atrium.

chapters.title: Pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum
chapters.summary: Right-to-left flow through an interatrial communication. The interatrial communication is the right atrium’s exit to the left heart; its restriction can add to the circulatory problem.

chapters.title: Tricuspid atresia
chapters.summary: Left-axis deviation with adult-like precordial progression and right atrial P waves. The source summary describes left-axis deviation, counterclockwise depolarization, adult precordial progression and right atrial P waves in this common arrangement.

chapters.title: The univentricular heart
chapters.summary: A morphologically defined single ventricular connection. The chapter defines the anatomy by atrial and AV connections to one main ventricular chamber, distinguishing it from other functionally single-ventricle categories.

chapters.title: Complete transposition of the great arteries
chapters.summary: A prominent right atrium and convex enlarged left ventricle shape the silhouette. The right atrium forms the blunter right border and the enlarged left ventricle the convex left border; arterial arrangement contributes to the narrow pedicle.

chapters.title: Truncus arteriosus
chapters.summary: Truncus arteriosus. A single great artery and single semilunar valve supply the three circulations.

chapters.title: Congenital anomalies of vena caval connection
chapters.summary: The route is usually physiologically harmless despite coronary sinus dilation. Blood still reaches the right atrium through the coronary sinus, so an isolated connection need not create a physiologic derangement.

chapters.title: Congenital pulmonary arteriovenous fistula
chapters.summary: Blood bypasses gas exchange while flow through uninvolved lung may fall reciprocally. The right-to-left intrapulmonary route bypasses the capillary bed; redistribution can limit the net increase in ventricular flow.

chapters.title: Hypoplastic left heart
chapters.summary: Right ventricle through pulmonary trunk, ductus and descending aorta. The pulmonary artery/ductus/descending aortic continuity provides systemic flow; retrograde flow supplies the small ascending aorta and coronary origins.

chapters.title: Congenital anomalies of the coronary circulation
chapters.summary: Whether its course is anterior, retroaortic, interarterial or intramyocardial. The source emphasizes that the route relative to the great arteries can be more important than the ectopic origin itself.

etiology.label: A changing condition
etiology.text: Congenital anatomy can acquire changing physiologic expression over time. A congenital malformation may evolve during gestation and extrauterine life; a bicuspid valve can become stenotic decades after birth.

epidemiology.label: Birth changes the physiology
epidemiology.text: Lung expansion and falling pulmonary vascular resistance redistribute flow. Lung expansion, rising oxygen tension, reduced pulmonary resistance and elimination of the placental circulation substantially alter cardiovascular physiology.

diagnostics.label: Flexible examination sequence
diagnostics.text: Examine while calm and integrate the history and other findings afterward. The depth and synthesis of analysis matter more than a rigid order; examining an infant during a calm interval may improve the assessment.

etiology.label: The vibratory childhood murmur
etiology.text: A Still murmur. The typical Still murmur is vibratory or buzzing, midsystolic and most prominent between the apex and lower left sternal edge in the supine child.

epidemiology.label: Position-dependent continuous sound
epidemiology.text: A cervical venous hum. Recumbency, neutral neck position and reduced jugular flow can diminish or abolish the venous hum.

diagnostics.label: Association is not a settled mechanism
diagnostics.text: Band prevalence persists across ages while Still murmur prevalence falls toward adolescence. The mismatch between age-related murmur prevalence and band prevalence, and the source’s explicit uncertainty, prevent treating the association as a settled universal mechanism.

epidemiology.label: Mirror-image arrangement
epidemiology.text: Situs inversus with dextrocardia. The described heart and abdominal viscera are in the mirror-image positions of the usual arrangement.

diagnostics.label: Isomerism is a morphologic descriptor
diagnostics.text: Right isomerism. Right isomerism describes bilateral morphologically right characteristics in structures normally different on the two sides.

etiology.text: Transplacental transfer of maternal IgG with injury to fetal conduction tissue. The source describes passive autoimmunity involving maternal IgG antibodies, including Ro/SSA and La/SSB associations; maternal lupus can become apparent only later.

epidemiology.label: Cannon venous waves
epidemiology.text: Right atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve. Independent atrial and ventricular activity can bring atrial contraction against the closed tricuspid valve, abruptly amplifying the venous A wave.

diagnostics.label: Normal radiography does not exclude block
diagnostics.text: Assess the atrial–ventricular relationship on a standard ECG. The radiographic appearance can be normal; the source emphasizes the standard ECG for establishing complete heart block.

atlas.summary: Herniation of the left atrial appendage through a partial left pericardial defect. Partial absence of the left pericardium may permit left atrial appendage herniation, producing the described convex left-border shadow.

etiology.label: A focal left-border bulge
etiology.text: Herniation of the left atrial appendage through a partial left pericardial defect. Partial absence of the left pericardium may permit left atrial appendage herniation, producing the described convex left-border shadow.

epidemiology.label: Confirm the anatomy
epidemiology.text: Thoracic CT or cardiac MRI. The source identifies CT and MRI as definitive modalities; echocardiography may suggest complete absence and identify coexisting defects.

diagnostics.label: Constraint and right-sided dimensions
diagnostics.text: Reduced pericardial restraint particularly affects the relatively thin-walled right-sided chambers. Loss of normal pericardial constraint particularly affects the right ventricle and right atrium and can alter systemic venous return and septal motion.

atlas.summary: Atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial discordance. Two discordant junctions place systemic venous blood in the pulmonary circuit and pulmonary venous blood in the systemic circuit, so the circulations are in series.

etiology.label: Double discordance
etiology.text: Atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial discordance. Two discordant junctions place systemic venous blood in the pulmonary circuit and pulmonary venous blood in the systemic circuit, so the circulations are in series.

epidemiology.label: Systemic atrioventricular valve
epidemiology.text: Morphologic tricuspid valve. The inverted left atrioventricular valve is morphologically tricuspid; Ebstein-like abnormalities and age-related regurgitation are important.

diagnostics.label: Reversed septal activation
diagnostics.text: Q waves in right precordial leads with absent left precordial Q waves. Inverted bundle branches activate the septum from right to left, reversing the usual precordial septal Q-wave pattern.

atlas.summary: A mobile stenotic aortic valve. The sound arises from abrupt movement of a mobile doming valve and identifies valvar level rather than degree.

etiology.label: Localizing an ejection sound
etiology.text: A mobile stenotic aortic valve. The sound arises from abrupt movement of a mobile doming valve and identifies valvar level rather than degree.

epidemiology.label: Imaging a bicuspid valve
epidemiology.text: Image the open valve for two unequal doming leaflets and an elliptical orifice. Open-valve imaging reveals the bicuspid anatomy that can be obscured by a false raphe during closure.

diagnostics.label: Acute regurgitation can sound soft
diagnostics.text: Relatively low regurgitant flow velocity can make severe acute disease acoustically unimpressive. The source describes short, medium-pitched, disarmingly soft murmurs in acute severe regurgitation; chronic peripheral signs may be absent.

etiology.label: Arm–leg examination
etiology.text: Compare upper-extremity and femoral pulses and blood pressures. Upper–lower extremity pulse and pressure differences are hallmarks; brachial–femoral comparison is particularly practical in infants.

epidemiology.label: Age and collateral signs
epidemiology.text: Notching usually develops later through enlarged posterior intercostal collateral arteries. Collateral posterior intercostal arteries produce notching, which seldom appears before age six years.

diagnostics.label: Distal perfusion in interrupted arch
diagnostics.text: Pulmonary trunk through a patent ductus into the descending aorta. Pulmonary trunk–ductus–descending aortic continuity can supply the lower body; diminishing femoral pulses can signal ductal constriction.

atlas.title: Congenital obstruction to left atrial flow: Mitral stenosis, cor triatriatum, pulmonary vein stenosis
atlas.summary: Parachute mitral valve. A single papillary muscle receiving all chordae defines the parachute arrangement and can restrict interchordal flow.

etiology.label: Parachute apparatus
etiology.text: Parachute mitral valve. A single papillary muscle receiving all chordae defines the parachute arrangement and can restrict interchordal flow.

epidemiology.label: An absent opening snap
epidemiology.text: The abnormal leaflet apparatus may not make the brisk opening and closing movements required for those sounds. The characteristic brisk motion of a mobile anterior leaflet is not a feature of the congenital lesion described.

diagnostics.label: Regional pulmonary venous congestion
diagnostics.text: Unequal stenosis of individual pulmonary veins proximal to the left atrium. Individual veins can have different severities of narrowing, producing regional congestion while the downstream left atrium remains normal-sized.

atlas.title: Congenital pulmonary stenosis and regurgitation
atlas.summary: Dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis. Dysplastic pulmonary stenosis has thickened separate poorly mobile leaflets without commissural fusion.

etiology.label: Valve morphology
etiology.text: Dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis. Dysplastic pulmonary stenosis has thickened separate poorly mobile leaflets without commissural fusion.

epidemiology.label: Critical obstruction with a soft murmur
epidemiology.text: Pinpoint pulmonary stenosis can have a deceptively soft murmur. The source emphasizes that pinpoint neonatal stenosis may sound disarmingly soft despite severe obstruction.

diagnostics.label: Low-pressure regurgitant sound
diagnostics.text: Short delayed low-to-medium-frequency crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the upper left sternal border. The source describes a distinctive short delayed low-to-medium-frequency diastolic murmur, sometimes louder with inspiration.

atlas.title: Ebstein’s anomaly of the tricuspid valve
atlas.summary: The inlet right ventricle between the anatomic annulus and displaced functional valve. Apical displacement atrializes the proximal inlet right ventricle while the trabecular and outlet portions form the functional right ventricle.

etiology.label: Apical valve displacement
etiology.text: The inlet right ventricle between the anatomic annulus and displaced functional valve. Apical displacement atrializes the proximal inlet right ventricle while the trabecular and outlet portions form the functional right ventricle.

epidemiology.label: Changing cyanosis across life
epidemiology.text: A neonatal right-to-left atrial shunt can diminish as pulmonary resistance falls and reappear when abnormal right ventricular filling pressure rises. The source describes this uncommon course through changing right-sided filling conditions and interatrial shunting.

diagnostics.label: Defining anatomy and shunt
diagnostics.text: Identify a PFO or secundum defect and determine interatrial shunt direction. Color flow imaging and Doppler identify the atrial pathway and whether right-to-left shunting coexists.

atlas.title: Atrial septal defect: Simple and complex
atlas.summary: Relative compliance of the two ventricles. With little atrial pressure difference, preferential filling of the more compliant right ventricle produces the usual left-to-right shunt.

etiology.label: Shunt and ventricular compliance
etiology.text: Relative compliance of the two ventricles. With little atrial pressure difference, preferential filling of the more compliant right ventricle produces the usual left-to-right shunt.

epidemiology.label: Fixed versus persistent splitting
epidemiology.text: Wide fixed splitting. Fixed denotes unchanged separation with respiration; persistent splitting remains audible but varies in width.

diagnostics.label: Bridging leaflets and shunt levels
diagnostics.text: Communication at both atrial and ventricular levels. Free-floating bridging leaflets permit both atrial and ventricular components of the complete canal.

atlas.title: Pulmonary stenosis with interatrial communication
atlas.summary: Patent foramen ovale. Severe pulmonary stenosis with right-to-left shunting most often uses a patent foramen ovale; a nonrestrictive secundum defect more often accompanies mild-to-moderate stenosis and left-to-right flow.

etiology.label: Anatomic-physiologic pairing
etiology.text: Patent foramen ovale. Severe pulmonary stenosis with right-to-left shunting most often uses a patent foramen ovale; a nonrestrictive secundum defect more often accompanies mild-to-moderate stenosis and left-to-right flow.

epidemiology.label: Central versus peripheral cyanosis
epidemiology.text: A low-skin-flow peripheral component has improved; central shunt cyanosis must still be assessed. Warmth improves skin blood flow and can diminish peripheral cyanosis while making any persistent central component easier to recognize.

diagnostics.label: Anatomy, gradient and shunt direction
diagnostics.text: Doppler for the obstructive gradient and color flow for the interatrial shunt. Imaging identifies the valve and interatrial pathway; Doppler assesses the gradient and color flow confirms shunt direction.

atlas.title: Ventricular septal defect
atlas.summary: Restrictive defect. Restriction at the defect limits pressure transmission and shunt flow, leaving a systolic pressure difference.

etiology.label: Restriction and pressure
etiology.text: Restrictive defect. Restriction at the defect limits pressure transmission and shunt flow, leaving a systolic pressure difference.

epidemiology.label: Shunt reversal
epidemiology.text: Right-to-left shunting from pulmonary vascular disease. With equal ventricular systolic pressures, relative vascular resistances govern flow; suprasystemic pulmonary resistance favors reversal.

diagnostics.label: Associated aortic leakage
diagnostics.text: Aortic cusp prolapse and regurgitation. Perimembranous and subarterial defects can be associated with aortic cusp prolapse; regurgitant volume can explain disproportionate left ventricular enlargement.

atlas.title: Ventricular septal defect with pulmonary stenosis
atlas.summary: Anterior and cephalad deviation of the infundibular septum. Outlet septal malalignment creates the ventricular defect, narrows right ventricular outflow and contributes to aortic override.

etiology.label: Unifying anatomy
etiology.text: Anterior and cephalad deviation of the infundibular septum. Outlet septal malalignment creates the ventricular defect, narrows right ventricular outflow and contributes to aortic override.

epidemiology.label: A murmur during deterioration
epidemiology.text: A sharp decline in forward pulmonary blood flow. Less blood traverses the stenotic pulmonary outflow, so the murmur shortens and softens despite worsening hypoxemia.

diagnostics.label: Pressure ceiling and its exception
diagnostics.text: The ventricle can decompress through the communication into the systemic outlet. The nonrestrictive defect imposes a systemic pressure ceiling; partial occlusion or true restriction can remove that protection.

atlas.title: Double outlet ventricle
atlas.summary: Double outlet right ventricle. The chapter uses ventricular support of most of both arterial valves as its pragmatic definition while acknowledging classification debates.

etiology.label: Pragmatic anatomic definition
etiology.text: Double outlet right ventricle. The chapter uses ventricular support of most of both arterial valves as its pragmatic definition while acknowledging classification debates.

epidemiology.label: Subaortic physiology
epidemiology.text: A large ventricular left-to-right shunt with increased pulmonary flow. Low pulmonary resistance permits increased pulmonary flow and left ventricular volume overload, resembling a large isolated ventricular defect.

diagnostics.label: The ventricular exit
diagnostics.text: Obstruction to left ventricular egress and subaortic flow. The communication is an essential left ventricular exit; restriction can act as subaortic stenosis rather than a uniformly favorable reduction in shunt.

atlas.title: Patent ductus arteriosus and aortopulmonary window
atlas.summary: Patent ductus arteriosus. The normal ductal insertion is near the left pulmonary artery, with its aortic end distal to the left subclavian artery.

etiology.label: Ductal anatomy
etiology.text: Patent ductus arteriosus. The normal ductal insertion is near the left pulmonary artery, with its aortic end distal to the left subclavian artery.

epidemiology.label: Continuous flow and sound
epidemiology.text: Classic continuous ductal murmur. The classic ductal sound envelops the second heart sound with continuous systolic-to-diastolic flow.

diagnostics.label: Window versus ductus
diagnostics.text: Desaturated blood enters proximal to systemic arch distribution. A window delivers blood into the ascending aorta, unlike the usual distal ductal insertion.

atlas.title: Anomalous origin of the left coronary artery from the pulmonary trunk
atlas.summary: Falling pulmonary pressure reduces antegrade perfusion through the anomalous artery. Initially high pulmonary pressure can support antegrade flow. Its postnatal fall reduces that supply unless intercoronary perfusion becomes adequate.

etiology.label: Postnatal perfusion transition
etiology.text: Falling pulmonary pressure reduces antegrade perfusion through the anomalous artery. Initially high pulmonary pressure can support antegrade flow. Its postnatal fall reduces that supply unless intercoronary perfusion becomes adequate.

epidemiology.label: Ischemic valve dysfunction
epidemiology.text: Ischemic papillary muscle dysfunction. Papillary muscle ischemia can impair mitral competence and add regurgitant volume to an already compromised ventricle.

diagnostics.label: Imaging the coronary pathway
diagnostics.text: Define whether the left coronary arises from the pulmonary trunk or from its normal aortic sinus. An anomalous left coronary lacks its normal aortic origin; a coronary arterial fistula can have similar pulmonary flow while both coronary arteries retain aortic origins.

atlas.title: Congenital coronary arterial fistula
atlas.summary: Congenital coronary arterial fistula. A fistulous branch provides an abnormal drainage route despite usually appropriate coronary origins.

etiology.label: Fistulous anatomy
etiology.text: Congenital coronary arterial fistula. A fistulous branch provides an abnormal drainage route despite usually appropriate coronary origins.

epidemiology.label: Ischemia despite a small shunt
epidemiology.text: Low-resistance runoff can divert coronary blood away from myocardium. Myocardial steal depends on the low-resistance alternative pathway and the coronary territory involved, not only total pulmonary shunt size.

diagnostics.label: Left ventricular drainage
diagnostics.text: Aortic-to-ventricular pressure difference favors diastolic fistulous flow. A coronary-to-left ventricular communication can produce an early diastolic murmur; systolic flow depends on the stoma and compression pattern.

atlas.title: Congenital aneurysms of the sinuses of valsalva
atlas.summary: Right atrium. The noncoronary sinus is anatomically related to the right atrium; right coronary sinus aneurysms commonly enter the right ventricle or sometimes the right atrium.

etiology.label: Anatomy predicts rupture site
etiology.text: Right atrium. The noncoronary sinus is anatomically related to the right atrium; right coronary sinus aneurysms commonly enter the right ventricle or sometimes the right atrium.

epidemiology.label: New continuous sound
epidemiology.text: Rupture of a coexisting sinus of Valsalva aneurysm. The source highlights this change as a clue to an aortic sinus aneurysm rupturing into the right side of the heart.

diagnostics.label: Septal extension and conduction
diagnostics.text: Injury to the AV node or His bundle near the septal base. Ruptured or unruptured aneurysms penetrating the septal base can disrupt nearby conduction tissue.

atlas.title: Pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum
atlas.summary: Right-to-left flow through an interatrial communication. The interatrial communication is the right atrium’s exit to the left heart; its restriction can add to the circulatory problem.

etiology.label: Obligatory atrial pathway
etiology.text: Right-to-left flow through an interatrial communication. The interatrial communication is the right atrium’s exit to the left heart; its restriction can add to the circulatory problem.

epidemiology.label: Variable right-heart anatomy
epidemiology.text: Both patterns occur, and tricuspid competence helps explain their different appearances. The chapter describes a common small-ventricle pattern and a less common dilated pattern associated with an incompetent dysplastic or Ebstein-like valve.

diagnostics.label: ECG and the small ventricle
diagnostics.text: The small cavity can generate little right ventricular electrical amplitude despite its thick wall. The source describes absent prominent RV hypertrophy voltage in the small-ventricle pattern; chamber geometry and cavity size matter.

atlas.title: Tricuspid atresia
atlas.summary: Left-axis deviation with adult-like precordial progression and right atrial P waves. The source summary describes left-axis deviation, counterclockwise depolarization, adult precordial progression and right atrial P waves in this common arrangement.

etiology.label: Obligatory atrial escape
etiology.text: Right-to-left flow across an interatrial communication. Systemic venous blood must cross from right atrium to left atrium and pass through the patent left AV valve.

epidemiology.label: Arterial relationship
epidemiology.text: Subaortic obstruction to systemic output. In this arrangement left ventricular blood must traverse the defect to reach the transposed aorta; restriction creates subaortic stenosis.

diagnostics.label: Defining the anatomy
diagnostics.text: Echocardiography with color flow and Doppler. Echo identifies the echodense absent connection, chamber sizes, great arterial relationships and shunt or obstruction physiology.

atlas.title: The univentricular heart
atlas.summary: A morphologically defined single ventricular connection. The chapter defines the anatomy by atrial and AV connections to one main ventricular chamber, distinguishing it from other functionally single-ventricle categories.

etiology.label: Morphologic definition
etiology.text: A morphologically defined single ventricular connection. The chapter defines the anatomy by atrial and AV connections to one main ventricular chamber, distinguishing it from other functionally single-ventricle categories.

epidemiology.label: Streaming
epidemiology.text: Preferential streaming can direct oxygenated blood toward the aorta. The source describes partial stream separation influenced by outlet arrangement and pulmonary resistance.

diagnostics.label: Recognizing severity
diagnostics.text: Less blood crosses the increasingly obstructed pulmonary outlet. As stenosis increases, more flow is diverted to the systemic outlet and less traverses the pulmonary obstruction, reducing its murmur.

atlas.title: Complete transposition of the great arteries
atlas.summary: A prominent right atrium and convex enlarged left ventricle shape the silhouette. The right atrium forms the blunter right border and the enlarged left ventricle the convex left border; arterial arrangement contributes to the narrow pedicle.

etiology.label: Connection and circulation
etiology.text: AV concordance with ventriculoarterial discordance and parallel circuits. Complete transposition combines AV concordance and ventriculoarterial discordance, creating parallel systemic and pulmonary recirculation.

epidemiology.label: Normal early tests
epidemiology.text: A normal early ECG does not exclude the abnormal arterial connections. The chapter explicitly describes a potentially normal ECG in the first days; structural assessment remains essential.

diagnostics.label: Radiographic recognition
diagnostics.text: A prominent right atrium and convex enlarged left ventricle shape the silhouette. The right atrium forms the blunter right border and the enlarged left ventricle the convex left border; arterial arrangement contributes to the narrow pedicle.

atlas.title: Truncus arteriosus
atlas.summary: Truncus arteriosus. A single great artery and single semilunar valve supply the three circulations.

etiology.label: Single arterial outlet
etiology.text: Truncus arteriosus. A single great artery and single semilunar valve supply the three circulations.

epidemiology.label: Cyanosis and congestion
epidemiology.text: Falling pulmonary resistance increases lung flow and ventricular volume load. More pulmonary flow improves systemic oxygenation but imposes volume overload and may cause severe heart failure.

diagnostics.label: Associated phenotype
diagnostics.text: DiGeorge syndrome. The chapter describes DiGeorge-related thymic and parathyroid deficiency with truncus arteriosus.

atlas.title: Congenital anomalies of vena caval connection
atlas.summary: The route is usually physiologically harmless despite coronary sinus dilation. Blood still reaches the right atrium through the coronary sinus, so an isolated connection need not create a physiologic derangement.

etiology.label: Benign venous route
etiology.text: The route is usually physiologically harmless despite coronary sinus dilation. Blood still reaches the right atrium through the coronary sinus, so an isolated connection need not create a physiologic derangement.

epidemiology.label: Interrupted inferior cava
epidemiology.text: Azygos continuation, which can be physiologically insignificant in isolation. The interrupted inferior caval flow continues through a dilated azygos system to the right SVC; isolated cases need not cause a shunt.

diagnostics.label: Cyanosis without RV overload
diagnostics.text: Right-heart flow is normal or reduced because some systemic venous blood bypasses it. Anomalous caval return bypasses the right heart, unlike lesions with major RV pressure or volume overload.

atlas.title: Congenital pulmonary arteriovenous fistula
atlas.summary: Blood bypasses gas exchange while flow through uninvolved lung may fall reciprocally. The right-to-left intrapulmonary route bypasses the capillary bed; redistribution can limit the net increase in ventricular flow.

etiology.label: Bypassing gas exchange
etiology.text: Blood bypasses gas exchange while flow through uninvolved lung may fall reciprocally. The right-to-left intrapulmonary route bypasses the capillary bed; redistribution can limit the net increase in ventricular flow.

epidemiology.label: Auscultatory localization
epidemiology.text: A peripheral pulmonary fistula can generate a localized flow murmur. Peripheral fistulae transmit sounds to the overlying chest wall; inspiratory flow and reduced compression may increase audibility.

diagnostics.label: Neurologic risk
diagnostics.text: Paradoxical embolism, stroke and brain abscess. The shunt bypasses the pulmonary filter; the source highlights embolic events and brain abscess.

atlas.title: Hypoplastic left heart
atlas.summary: Right ventricle through pulmonary trunk, ductus and descending aorta. The pulmonary artery/ductus/descending aortic continuity provides systemic flow; retrograde flow supplies the small ascending aorta and coronary origins.

etiology.label: Systemic route
etiology.text: Right ventricle through pulmonary trunk, ductus and descending aorta. The pulmonary artery/ductus/descending aortic continuity provides systemic flow; retrograde flow supplies the small ascending aorta and coronary origins.

epidemiology.label: Oxygen delivery
epidemiology.text: Flow is preferentially diverted to the lungs at the expense of systemic output. The right ventricle supplies both beds; increasing lung flow can improve mixing saturation while reducing systemic blood flow.

diagnostics.label: Atrial exit
diagnostics.text: Pulmonary venous return encounters an obstructed left atrium. The left atrium needs an alternative exit when mitral inflow is severely limited; atrial restriction compromises that exit and promotes congestion.

atlas.title: Congenital anomalies of the coronary circulation
atlas.summary: Whether its course is anterior, retroaortic, interarterial or intramyocardial. The source emphasizes that the route relative to the great arteries can be more important than the ectopic origin itself.

etiology.label: Origin versus course
etiology.text: Whether its course is anterior, retroaortic, interarterial or intramyocardial. The source emphasizes that the route relative to the great arteries can be more important than the ectopic origin itself.

epidemiology.label: Absent versus atretic
epidemiology.text: Absence of a common left main trunk, generally functionally benign. Separate patent LAD and circumflex origins are different from a blind or imperforate left main origin.

diagnostics.label: Collateral dependence
diagnostics.text: Adequate channels from a normally arising right coronary artery. Survival depends on adequate connections from the right coronary artery to the distal left system; presentation can span infancy to adulthood.

therapies.text: Congenital anatomy can acquire changing physiologic expression over time. A congenital malformation may evolve during gestation and extrauterine life; a bicuspid valve can become stenotic decades after birth.
therapies.title: Introduction: Formulation of the problem

therapies.text: Congenital functional abnormalities can exist without a gross structural defect. The source includes congenital complete heart block among functionally significant conditions that need not be gross structural defects.
therapies.title: Introduction: Formulation of the problem

therapies.text: Lung expansion and falling pulmonary vascular resistance redistribute flow. Lung expansion, rising oxygen tension, reduced pulmonary resistance and elimination of the placental circulation substantially alter cardiovascular physiology.
therapies.title: Introduction: Formulation of the problem

therapies.text: Integrate the imaging with prior clinical observations and predicted physiology. The diagnostic approach synthesizes history, examination, ECG, radiography and advanced imaging into a coherent anatomic–physiologic explanation.
therapies.title: Introduction: Formulation of the problem

therapies.text: Examine while calm and integrate the history and other findings afterward. The depth and synthesis of analysis matter more than a rigid order; examining an infant during a calm interval may improve the assessment.
therapies.title: Introduction: Formulation of the problem

therapies.text: A Still murmur. The typical Still murmur is vibratory or buzzing, midsystolic and most prominent between the apex and lower left sternal edge in the supine child.
therapies.title: Functional murmurs

therapies.text: Transient disparity between the pulmonary trunk and its branch sizes. The neonatal pulmonary trunk–branch size disparity and branch geometry can produce widely transmitted systolic turbulence; the murmur alone does not distinguish transient physiology from fixed branch stenosis.
therapies.title: Functional murmurs

therapies.text: A cervical venous hum. Recumbency, neutral neck position and reduced jugular flow can diminish or abolish the venous hum.
therapies.title: Functional murmurs

therapies.text: Flow vibrations near the origins of the major brachiocephalic arteries. The supraclavicular arterial murmur is systolic, maximal above the clavicles and may diminish or disappear with shoulder hyperextension.
therapies.title: Functional murmurs

therapies.text: Band prevalence persists across ages while Still murmur prevalence falls toward adolescence. The mismatch between age-related murmur prevalence and band prevalence, and the source’s explicit uncertainty, prevent treating the association as a settled universal mechanism.
therapies.section: Association is not a settled mechanism
therapies.title: Functional murmurs

therapies.text: Secondary cardiac displacement. Cardiac displacement is a secondary shift in intrathoracic position, such as one produced by diaphragmatic eventration.
therapies.title: The cardiac malpositions

therapies.text: Identify the atria, valves, ventricles and arterial connections systematically. The source describes systematic attention to morphology, atrioventricular connections, ventriculoarterial connections and great-artery relationships.
therapies.title: The cardiac malpositions

therapies.text: Situs inversus with dextrocardia. The described heart and abdominal viscera are in the mirror-image positions of the usual arrangement.
therapies.title: The cardiac malpositions

therapies.text: Two discordant connections restore the appropriate destinations of blood. Atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial discordance can together produce physiologic correction of blood-flow destinations.
therapies.section: The effect of two discordant connections
therapies.title: The cardiac malpositions

therapies.text: Right isomerism. Right isomerism describes bilateral morphologically right characteristics in structures normally different on the two sides.
therapies.title: The cardiac malpositions

therapies.text: Transplacental transfer of maternal IgG with injury to fetal conduction tissue. The source describes passive autoimmunity involving maternal IgG antibodies, including Ro/SSA and La/SSB associations; maternal lupus can become apparent only later.
therapies.title: Isolated congenital complete heart block

therapies.text: Atrial and ventricular activation are independent. In complete heart block, P waves and QRS complexes occur independently, rather than maintaining a fixed conducted relationship.
therapies.title: Isolated congenital complete heart block

therapies.text: Right atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve. Independent atrial and ventricular activity can bring atrial contraction against the closed tricuspid valve, abruptly amplifying the venous A wave.
therapies.title: Isolated congenital complete heart block

therapies.text: The changing atrial–ventricular timing alters valve position at ventricular systole. Because atria and ventricles beat independently, the PR relationship changes and first-sound intensity can vary widely.
therapies.title: Isolated congenital complete heart block

therapies.text: Assess the atrial–ventricular relationship on a standard ECG. The radiographic appearance can be normal; the source emphasizes the standard ECG for establishing complete heart block.
therapies.section: Normal radiography does not exclude block
therapies.title: Isolated congenital complete heart block

therapies.text: Herniation of the left atrial appendage through a partial left pericardial defect. Partial absence of the left pericardium may permit left atrial appendage herniation, producing the described convex left-border shadow.
therapies.title: Congenital abnormalities of the pericardium

therapies.text: Loss of normal pericardial restraint. Complete absence can produce striking cardiac mobility, leftward/posterior displacement and interposed lung tissue.
therapies.title: Congenital abnormalities of the pericardium

therapies.text: Thoracic CT or cardiac MRI. The source identifies CT and MRI as definitive modalities; echocardiography may suggest complete absence and identify coexisting defects.
therapies.title: Congenital abnormalities of the pericardium

therapies.text: A congenital pericardial cyst. A congenital pericardial cyst typically forms a smooth homogeneous density at the right cardiophrenic angle.
therapies.title: Congenital abnormalities of the pericardium

therapies.text: Reduced pericardial restraint particularly affects the relatively thin-walled right-sided chambers. Loss of normal pericardial constraint particularly affects the right ventricle and right atrium and can alter systemic venous return and septal motion.
therapies.title: Congenital abnormalities of the pericardium

therapies.text: Atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial discordance. Two discordant junctions place systemic venous blood in the pulmonary circuit and pulmonary venous blood in the systemic circuit, so the circulations are in series.
therapies.title: Congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries

therapies.text: The systemic morphologic right ventricle must sustain a workload for which its usual geometry and blood supply are not designed. The systemic right ventricle retains right-ventricular geometry and a morphologically right coronary supply despite systemic loading.
therapies.title: Congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries

therapies.text: Morphologic tricuspid valve. The inverted left atrioventricular valve is morphologically tricuspid; Ebstein-like abnormalities and age-related regurgitation are important.
therapies.title: Congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries

therapies.text: Replacement of conduction fibers by fibrous tissue in the long penetrating bundle. Fibrous replacement in the long penetrating bundle contributes to age-related atrioventricular block; defects may occur at several conduction levels.
therapies.title: Congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries

therapies.text: Q waves in right precordial leads with absent left precordial Q waves. Inverted bundle branches activate the septum from right to left, reversing the usual precordial septal Q-wave pattern.
therapies.title: Congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries

therapies.text: A mobile stenotic aortic valve. The sound arises from abrupt movement of a mobile doming valve and identifies valvar level rather than degree.
therapies.title: Congenital aortic stenosis: Congenital aortic regurgitation

therapies.text: Reduced murmur intensity does not establish reduced obstruction. Aortic stenosis murmur intensity can decrease in left ventricular failure; loudness is not a stand-alone measure of obstruction.
therapies.section: A quiet murmur in ventricular failure
therapies.title: Congenital aortic stenosis: Congenital aortic regurgitation

therapies.text: Image the open valve for two unequal doming leaflets and an elliptical orifice. Open-valve imaging reveals the bicuspid anatomy that can be obscured by a false raphe during closure.
therapies.title: Congenital aortic stenosis: Congenital aortic regurgitation

therapies.text: Rapid rise, wide pulse pressure and brisk collapse. Chronic severe regurgitation produces a rapid upstroke, wide pulse pressure, sometimes a bisferiens peak, and brisk collapse.
therapies.title: Congenital aortic stenosis: Congenital aortic regurgitation

therapies.text: Relatively low regurgitant flow velocity can make severe acute disease acoustically unimpressive. The source describes short, medium-pitched, disarmingly soft murmurs in acute severe regurgitation; chronic peripheral signs may be absent.
therapies.title: Congenital aortic stenosis: Congenital aortic regurgitation

therapies.text: Compare upper-extremity and femoral pulses and blood pressures. Upper–lower extremity pulse and pressure differences are hallmarks; brachial–femoral comparison is particularly practical in infants.
therapies.title: Coarctation of the aorta and interrupted aortic arch

therapies.text: A stiff, poorly distensible precoarctation aorta. Increased collagen and reduced smooth muscle stiffen the proximal aorta, contributing to systolic hypertension and baroreceptor resetting.
therapies.title: Coarctation of the aorta and interrupted aortic arch

therapies.text: Notching usually develops later through enlarged posterior intercostal collateral arteries. Collateral posterior intercostal arteries produce notching, which seldom appears before age six years.
therapies.title: Coarctation of the aorta and interrupted aortic arch

therapies.text: Closure of the ductus arteriosus. The source specifically associates acute neonatal symptoms in severe coarctation with ductal closure.
therapies.title: Coarctation of the aorta and interrupted aortic arch

therapies.text: Pulmonary trunk through a patent ductus into the descending aorta. Pulmonary trunk–ductus–descending aortic continuity can supply the lower body; diminishing femoral pulses can signal ductal constriction.
therapies.title: Coarctation of the aorta and interrupted aortic arch

therapies.text: Parachute mitral valve. A single papillary muscle receiving all chordae defines the parachute arrangement and can restrict interchordal flow.
therapies.title: Congenital obstruction to left atrial flow: Mitral stenosis, cor triatriatum, pulmonary vein stenosis

therapies.text: Supravalvular mitral ring, parachute mitral valve, subaortic stenosis and coarctation. The classic four lesions are left-sided inflow/outflow obstructions; not all need be present or functionally significant.
therapies.title: Congenital obstruction to left atrial flow: Mitral stenosis, cor triatriatum, pulmonary vein stenosis

therapies.text: The abnormal leaflet apparatus may not make the brisk opening and closing movements required for those sounds. The characteristic brisk motion of a mobile anterior leaflet is not a feature of the congenital lesion described.
therapies.title: Congenital obstruction to left atrial flow: Mitral stenosis, cor triatriatum, pulmonary vein stenosis

therapies.text: Cor triatriatum. A membrane proximal to the appendage and valve distinguishes typical cor triatriatum from a supravalvular ring.
therapies.title: Congenital obstruction to left atrial flow: Mitral stenosis, cor triatriatum, pulmonary vein stenosis

therapies.text: Unequal stenosis of individual pulmonary veins proximal to the left atrium. Individual veins can have different severities of narrowing, producing regional congestion while the downstream left atrium remains normal-sized.
therapies.title: Congenital obstruction to left atrial flow: Mitral stenosis, cor triatriatum, pulmonary vein stenosis

therapies.text: Dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis. Dysplastic pulmonary stenosis has thickened separate poorly mobile leaflets without commissural fusion.
therapies.title: Congenital pulmonary stenosis and regurgitation

therapies.text: Reduced additional cephalad movement of a mobile pulmonary valve during ventricular contraction. Inspiration prepositions the mobile valve cephalad through increased right atrial contraction, reducing further excursion and the ejection sound.
therapies.title: Congenital pulmonary stenosis and regurgitation

therapies.text: Pinpoint pulmonary stenosis can have a deceptively soft murmur. The source emphasizes that pinpoint neonatal stenosis may sound disarmingly soft despite severe obstruction.
therapies.section: Critical obstruction with a soft murmur
therapies.title: Congenital pulmonary stenosis and regurgitation

therapies.text: The central pulmonary diastolic pressure can remain normal or nearly normal at valve closure. Branch stenosis can raise central systolic pressure while pressure falls to near-normal diastolic levels, so valve closure need not be accentuated.
therapies.section: Branch stenosis and the second sound
therapies.title: Congenital pulmonary stenosis and regurgitation

therapies.text: Short delayed low-to-medium-frequency crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the upper left sternal border. The source describes a distinctive short delayed low-to-medium-frequency diastolic murmur, sometimes louder with inspiration.
therapies.title: Congenital pulmonary stenosis and regurgitation

therapies.text: The inlet right ventricle between the anatomic annulus and displaced functional valve. Apical displacement atrializes the proximal inlet right ventricle while the trabecular and outlet portions form the functional right ventricle.
therapies.title: Ebstein’s anomaly of the tricuspid valve

therapies.text: A large compliant right atrium and toneless atrialized ventricle damp low-pressure regurgitant flow. Commodious right-sided chambers and low-pressure hypokinetic regurgitation can damp the expected jugular signs.
therapies.title: Ebstein’s anomaly of the tricuspid valve

therapies.text: A neonatal right-to-left atrial shunt can diminish as pulmonary resistance falls and reappear when abnormal right ventricular filling pressure rises. The source describes this uncommon course through changing right-sided filling conditions and interatrial shunting.
therapies.title: Ebstein’s anomaly of the tricuspid valve

therapies.text: Preexcitation. Early delta-wave inscription supports preexcitation; a short PR interval alone can occasionally occur without a delta wave or tachycardia history.
therapies.title: Ebstein’s anomaly of the tricuspid valve

therapies.text: Identify a PFO or secundum defect and determine interatrial shunt direction. Color flow imaging and Doppler identify the atrial pathway and whether right-to-left shunting coexists.
therapies.title: Ebstein’s anomaly of the tricuspid valve

therapies.text: Relative compliance of the two ventricles. With little atrial pressure difference, preferential filling of the more compliant right ventricle produces the usual left-to-right shunt.
therapies.title: Atrial septal defect: Simple and complex

therapies.text: Increased flow through the pulmonary outflow and pulmonary trunk. The systolic murmur reflects augmented pulmonary flow, not a high-velocity jet across the nonrestrictive atrial communication.
therapies.title: Atrial septal defect: Simple and complex

therapies.text: Wide fixed splitting. Fixed denotes unchanged separation with respiration; persistent splitting remains audible but varies in width.
therapies.title: Atrial septal defect: Simple and complex

therapies.text: Obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous connection. Obstructed anomalous venous return can produce severe neonatal hypoxemia and congestion with an unimpressive heart size and attenuated flow murmur.
therapies.title: Atrial septal defect: Simple and complex

therapies.text: Communication at both atrial and ventricular levels. Free-floating bridging leaflets permit both atrial and ventricular components of the complete canal.
therapies.title: Atrial septal defect: Simple and complex

therapies.text: Patent foramen ovale. Severe pulmonary stenosis with right-to-left shunting most often uses a patent foramen ovale; a nonrestrictive secundum defect more often accompanies mild-to-moderate stenosis and left-to-right flow.
therapies.title: Pulmonary stenosis with interatrial communication

therapies.text: High right atrial pressure stretches the foramen and drives blood toward the left atrium. Forceful atrial contraction raises right atrial pressure, increases PFO patency and can generate a presystolic right-to-left shunt.
therapies.title: Pulmonary stenosis with interatrial communication

therapies.text: A low-skin-flow peripheral component has improved; central shunt cyanosis must still be assessed. Warmth improves skin blood flow and can diminish peripheral cyanosis while making any persistent central component easier to recognize.
therapies.title: Pulmonary stenosis with interatrial communication

therapies.text: Coexisting mobile pulmonary valve stenosis. The combination adds valvar ejection sound, a longer louder stenotic murmur and further delay and softening of P2 to the atrial-shunt findings.
therapies.title: Pulmonary stenosis with interatrial communication

therapies.text: Doppler for the obstructive gradient and color flow for the interatrial shunt. Imaging identifies the valve and interatrial pathway; Doppler assesses the gradient and color flow confirms shunt direction.
therapies.title: Pulmonary stenosis with interatrial communication

therapies.text: Restrictive defect. Restriction at the defect limits pressure transmission and shunt flow, leaving a systolic pressure difference.
therapies.title: Ventricular septal defect

therapies.text: Falling pulmonary vascular resistance increases left-to-right flow. The neonatal fall in pulmonary resistance permits a larger shunt and pulmonary venous return, imposing left ventricular volume load.
therapies.title: Ventricular septal defect

therapies.text: Right-to-left shunting from pulmonary vascular disease. With equal ventricular systolic pressures, relative vascular resistances govern flow; suprasystemic pulmonary resistance favors reversal.
therapies.title: Ventricular septal defect

therapies.text: Reduced left-to-right flow can reflect worsening pulmonary vascular disease. As pulmonary resistance approaches systemic, the left-to-right murmur can shorten, soften and eventually disappear with reversal.
therapies.title: Ventricular septal defect

therapies.text: Aortic cusp prolapse and regurgitation. Perimembranous and subarterial defects can be associated with aortic cusp prolapse; regurgitant volume can explain disproportionate left ventricular enlargement.
therapies.title: Ventricular septal defect

therapies.text: Anterior and cephalad deviation of the infundibular septum. Outlet septal malalignment creates the ventricular defect, narrows right ventricular outflow and contributes to aortic override.
therapies.title: Ventricular septal defect with pulmonary stenosis

therapies.text: More right-to-left flow into the aorta and less pulmonary flow. Relative outflow and systemic resistances determine the balance; severe outflow obstruction diverts blood toward the aorta.
therapies.title: Ventricular septal defect with pulmonary stenosis

therapies.text: A sharp decline in forward pulmonary blood flow. Less blood traverses the stenotic pulmonary outflow, so the murmur shortens and softens despite worsening hypoxemia.
therapies.title: Ventricular septal defect with pulmonary stenosis

therapies.text: Increased systemic resistance and reduced return of desaturated leg blood. Squatting can redirect right ventricular flow toward the lungs and curtail desaturated lower-extremity venous return.
therapies.title: Ventricular septal defect with pulmonary stenosis

therapies.text: The ventricle can decompress through the communication into the systemic outlet. The nonrestrictive defect imposes a systemic pressure ceiling; partial occlusion or true restriction can remove that protection.
therapies.title: Ventricular septal defect with pulmonary stenosis

therapies.text: Double outlet right ventricle. The chapter uses ventricular support of most of both arterial valves as its pragmatic definition while acknowledging classification debates.
therapies.title: Double outlet ventricle

therapies.text: Left ventricular blood preferentially enters the pulmonary trunk. A subpulmonary communication directs left ventricular output toward the pulmonary outlet, creating a transposition-like physiology.
therapies.title: Double outlet ventricle

therapies.text: A large ventricular left-to-right shunt with increased pulmonary flow. Low pulmonary resistance permits increased pulmonary flow and left ventricular volume overload, resembling a large isolated ventricular defect.
therapies.title: Double outlet ventricle

therapies.text: Less pulmonary flow and more blood directed to the aorta. Obstruction diverts both ventricular streams away from the pulmonary outlet and toward the aorta, producing a tetralogy-like pattern.
therapies.title: Double outlet ventricle

therapies.text: Obstruction to left ventricular egress and subaortic flow. The communication is an essential left ventricular exit; restriction can act as subaortic stenosis rather than a uniformly favorable reduction in shunt.
therapies.title: Double outlet ventricle

therapies.text: Patent ductus arteriosus. The normal ductal insertion is near the left pulmonary artery, with its aortic end distal to the left subclavian artery.
therapies.title: Patent ductus arteriosus and aortopulmonary window

therapies.text: Increased pulmonary venous return imposes left ventricular volume load. Pulmonary recirculation returns to the left atrium and ventricle, increasing left-heart volume load.
therapies.title: Patent ductus arteriosus and aortopulmonary window

therapies.text: Classic continuous ductal murmur. The classic ductal sound envelops the second heart sound with continuous systolic-to-diastolic flow.
therapies.title: Patent ductus arteriosus and aortopulmonary window

therapies.text: Pulmonary arterial blood entering the descending aorta through a ductus distal to the right-arm supply. The ductal entry usually delivers desaturated blood to the lower body after the proximal arch vessels have branched.
therapies.title: Patent ductus arteriosus and aortopulmonary window

therapies.text: Desaturated blood enters proximal to systemic arch distribution. A window delivers blood into the ascending aorta, unlike the usual distal ductal insertion.
therapies.title: Patent ductus arteriosus and aortopulmonary window

therapies.text: Falling pulmonary pressure reduces antegrade perfusion through the anomalous artery. Initially high pulmonary pressure can support antegrade flow. Its postnatal fall reduces that supply unless intercoronary perfusion becomes adequate.
therapies.title: Anomalous origin of the left coronary artery from the pulmonary trunk

therapies.text: Collaterals restore some perfusion but also permit a low-resistance coronary steal. The collateral route can nourish myocardium while also bypassing capillaries toward a low-pressure pulmonary outlet.
therapies.title: Anomalous origin of the left coronary artery from the pulmonary trunk

therapies.text: Ischemic papillary muscle dysfunction. Papillary muscle ischemia can impair mitral competence and add regurgitant volume to an already compromised ventricle.
therapies.title: Anomalous origin of the left coronary artery from the pulmonary trunk

therapies.text: Anomalous left coronary artery from the pulmonary trunk. Deep narrow lateral q waves, often with left ventricular hypertrophy and a leftward axis, are a characteristic clue; early infant tracings can be less conspicuous.
therapies.title: Anomalous origin of the left coronary artery from the pulmonary trunk

therapies.text: Define whether the left coronary arises from the pulmonary trunk or from its normal aortic sinus. An anomalous left coronary lacks its normal aortic origin; a coronary arterial fistula can have similar pulmonary flow while both coronary arteries retain aortic origins.
therapies.title: Anomalous origin of the left coronary artery from the pulmonary trunk

therapies.text: Congenital coronary arterial fistula. A fistulous branch provides an abnormal drainage route despite usually appropriate coronary origins.
therapies.title: Congenital coronary arterial fistula

therapies.text: Left-to-right recirculation with right and left ventricular volume loading. Blood enters the right atrium and traverses the right heart, lungs and left heart before returning to the aorta.
therapies.title: Congenital coronary arterial fistula

therapies.text: Low-resistance runoff can divert coronary blood away from myocardium. Myocardial steal depends on the low-resistance alternative pathway and the coronary territory involved, not only total pulmonary shunt size.
therapies.title: Congenital coronary arterial fistula

therapies.text: The chamber or vessel receiving the fistula. The drainage site determines the intracardiac sound source and corresponding thoracic location.
therapies.title: Congenital coronary arterial fistula

therapies.text: Aortic-to-ventricular pressure difference favors diastolic fistulous flow. A coronary-to-left ventricular communication can produce an early diastolic murmur; systolic flow depends on the stoma and compression pattern.
therapies.title: Congenital coronary arterial fistula

therapies.text: Right atrium. The noncoronary sinus is anatomically related to the right atrium; right coronary sinus aneurysms commonly enter the right ventricle or sometimes the right atrium.
therapies.title: Congenital aneurysms of the sinuses of valsalva

therapies.text: The heart has little time to adapt to the acute shunt volume burden. Size, rapidity and receiving chamber determine the burden; sudden substantial recirculation can overwhelm adaptation.
therapies.title: Congenital aneurysms of the sinuses of valsalva

therapies.text: Rupture of a coexisting sinus of Valsalva aneurysm. The source highlights this change as a clue to an aortic sinus aneurysm rupturing into the right side of the heart.
therapies.title: Congenital aneurysms of the sinuses of valsalva

therapies.text: A ruptured aortic sinus communication is plausible. Sinus rupture murmurs can be continuous without the characteristic second-sound peak of the classic ductal murmur.
therapies.title: Congenital aneurysms of the sinuses of valsalva

therapies.text: Injury to the AV node or His bundle near the septal base. Ruptured or unruptured aneurysms penetrating the septal base can disrupt nearby conduction tissue.
therapies.title: Congenital aneurysms of the sinuses of valsalva

therapies.text: Right-to-left flow through an interatrial communication. The interatrial communication is the right atrium’s exit to the left heart; its restriction can add to the circulatory problem.
therapies.title: Pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum

therapies.text: Effective pulmonary blood flow can cease. The ductus supplies the pulmonary circuit in the usual anatomy; systemic-to-pulmonary collaterals are generally inadequate.
therapies.title: Pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum

therapies.text: Both patterns occur, and tricuspid competence helps explain their different appearances. The chapter describes a common small-ventricle pattern and a less common dilated pattern associated with an incompetent dysplastic or Ebstein-like valve.
therapies.title: Pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum

therapies.text: High right ventricular systolic pressure drives retrograde coronary flow. When aortic access is obstructed, myocardial perfusion can depend on suprasystemic right ventricular pressure supplying the coronary bed.
therapies.title: Pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum

therapies.text: The small cavity can generate little right ventricular electrical amplitude despite its thick wall. The source describes absent prominent RV hypertrophy voltage in the small-ventricle pattern; chamber geometry and cavity size matter.
therapies.title: Pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum

therapies.text: Right-to-left flow across an interatrial communication. Systemic venous blood must cross from right atrium to left atrium and pass through the patent left AV valve.
therapies.title: Tricuspid atresia

therapies.text: Increasing subpulmonary obstruction limits lung flow. With normally related arteries, the ventricular communication provides access to the pulmonary circuit; narrowing can produce acquired pulmonary atresia.
therapies.title: Tricuspid atresia

therapies.text: Subaortic obstruction to systemic output. In this arrangement left ventricular blood must traverse the defect to reach the transposed aorta; restriction creates subaortic stenosis.
therapies.title: Tricuspid atresia

therapies.text: Left-axis deviation with adult-like precordial progression and right atrial P waves. The source summary describes left-axis deviation, counterclockwise depolarization, adult precordial progression and right atrial P waves in this common arrangement.
therapies.title: Tricuspid atresia

therapies.text: Echocardiography with color flow and Doppler. Echo identifies the echodense absent connection, chamber sizes, great arterial relationships and shunt or obstruction physiology.
therapies.title: Tricuspid atresia

therapies.text: A morphologically defined single ventricular connection. The chapter defines the anatomy by atrial and AV connections to one main ventricular chamber, distinguishing it from other functionally single-ventricle categories.
therapies.title: The univentricular heart

therapies.text: Excess pulmonary flow with ventricular volume overload. Excess pulmonary flow produces heart failure and poor growth despite relatively mild cyanosis.
therapies.title: The univentricular heart

therapies.text: Preferential streaming can direct oxygenated blood toward the aorta. The source describes partial stream separation influenced by outlet arrangement and pulmonary resistance.
therapies.title: The univentricular heart

therapies.text: Subaortic obstruction with diversion toward the pulmonary circuit and greater volume burden. Restriction creates subaortic stenosis and may augment already excessive pulmonary flow and ventricular volume overload.
therapies.title: The univentricular heart

therapies.text: Less blood crosses the increasingly obstructed pulmonary outlet. As stenosis increases, more flow is diverted to the systemic outlet and less traverses the pulmonary obstruction, reducing its murmur.
therapies.title: The univentricular heart

therapies.text: AV concordance with ventriculoarterial discordance and parallel circuits. Complete transposition combines AV concordance and ventriculoarterial discordance, creating parallel systemic and pulmonary recirculation.
therapies.title: Complete transposition of the great arteries

therapies.text: Oxygenated blood recirculates through the pulmonary circuit instead of adequately entering systemic flow. An adequate communication permits exchange between the circuits; a restrictive atrial route can leave oxygenated blood trapped in pulmonary recirculation.
therapies.title: Complete transposition of the great arteries

therapies.text: A normal early ECG does not exclude the abnormal arterial connections. The chapter explicitly describes a potentially normal ECG in the first days; structural assessment remains essential.
therapies.title: Complete transposition of the great arteries

therapies.text: More oxygenated pulmonary arterial blood enters the descending aorta beyond the left subclavian artery. Oxygenated pulmonary arterial blood can pass through the ductus to the lower body, producing less cyanotic feet.
therapies.title: Complete transposition of the great arteries

therapies.text: A prominent right atrium and convex enlarged left ventricle shape the silhouette. The right atrium forms the blunter right border and the enlarged left ventricle the convex left border; arterial arrangement contributes to the narrow pedicle.
therapies.title: Complete transposition of the great arteries

therapies.text: Truncus arteriosus. A single great artery and single semilunar valve supply the three circulations.
therapies.title: Truncus arteriosus

therapies.text: Type 1 truncus. Type 1 has a short main pulmonary artery from the trunk; separate branch ostia constitute the other grouped pattern.
therapies.title: Truncus arteriosus

therapies.text: Falling pulmonary resistance increases lung flow and ventricular volume load. More pulmonary flow improves systemic oxygenation but imposes volume overload and may cause severe heart failure.
therapies.title: Truncus arteriosus

therapies.text: Regurgitant flow is received by both ventricles and adds to their burden. The biventricular truncus permits regurgitant volume to load both ventricles, adding to existing hemodynamic stress.
therapies.title: Truncus arteriosus

therapies.text: DiGeorge syndrome. The chapter describes DiGeorge-related thymic and parathyroid deficiency with truncus arteriosus.
therapies.title: Truncus arteriosus

therapies.text: The route is usually physiologically harmless despite coronary sinus dilation. Blood still reaches the right atrium through the coronary sinus, so an isolated connection need not create a physiologic derangement.
therapies.title: Congenital anomalies of vena caval connection

therapies.text: Left atrium to left SVC, across the bridge and into the right SVC. A freely communicating bridge can permit left-to-right flow from left atrium through the venous pathway to right atrium, reversing the expected cyanotic pattern.
therapies.title: Congenital anomalies of vena caval connection

therapies.text: Azygos continuation, which can be physiologically insignificant in isolation. The interrupted inferior caval flow continues through a dilated azygos system to the right SVC; isolated cases need not cause a shunt.
therapies.title: Congenital anomalies of vena caval connection

therapies.text: Persistent left superior vena cava. An unexpectedly enlarged coronary sinus can be the clue to an unsuspected left SVC; color and contrast studies define the route.
therapies.title: Congenital anomalies of vena caval connection

therapies.text: Right-heart flow is normal or reduced because some systemic venous blood bypasses it. Anomalous caval return bypasses the right heart, unlike lesions with major RV pressure or volume overload.
therapies.title: Congenital anomalies of vena caval connection

therapies.text: Blood bypasses gas exchange while flow through uninvolved lung may fall reciprocally. The right-to-left intrapulmonary route bypasses the capillary bed; redistribution can limit the net increase in ventricular flow.
therapies.title: Congenital pulmonary arteriovenous fistula

therapies.text: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia. The source describes an autosomal dominant vasculopathy with mucocutaneous bleeding and visceral arteriovenous malformations.
therapies.title: Congenital pulmonary arteriovenous fistula

therapies.text: A peripheral pulmonary fistula can generate a localized flow murmur. Peripheral fistulae transmit sounds to the overlying chest wall; inspiratory flow and reduced compression may increase audibility.
therapies.title: Congenital pulmonary arteriovenous fistula

therapies.text: A pulmonary right-to-left shunt. The chapter describes delayed appearance beyond three cycles as usually indicating pulmonary shunting; the timing is a clue interpreted with anatomy.
therapies.title: Congenital pulmonary arteriovenous fistula

therapies.text: Paradoxical embolism, stroke and brain abscess. The shunt bypasses the pulmonary filter; the source highlights embolic events and brain abscess.
therapies.title: Congenital pulmonary arteriovenous fistula

therapies.text: Right ventricle through pulmonary trunk, ductus and descending aorta. The pulmonary artery/ductus/descending aortic continuity provides systemic flow; retrograde flow supplies the small ascending aorta and coronary origins.
therapies.title: Hypoplastic left heart

therapies.text: Reduced systemic and retrograde coronary perfusion impairs output and RV function. The ductus supports systemic and coronary supply; constriction compromises both and can worsen the sole pumping ventricle.
therapies.title: Hypoplastic left heart

therapies.text: Flow is preferentially diverted to the lungs at the expense of systemic output. The right ventricle supplies both beds; increasing lung flow can improve mixing saturation while reducing systemic blood flow.
therapies.title: Hypoplastic left heart

therapies.text: A severe ductal-dependent left-heart lesion remains possible. The source emphasizes unimpressive auscultation despite dramatic illness; aortic atresia leaves a single pulmonary closure sound.
therapies.title: Hypoplastic left heart

therapies.text: Pulmonary venous return encounters an obstructed left atrium. The left atrium needs an alternative exit when mitral inflow is severely limited; atrial restriction compromises that exit and promotes congestion.
therapies.title: Hypoplastic left heart

therapies.text: Whether its course is anterior, retroaortic, interarterial or intramyocardial. The source emphasizes that the route relative to the great arteries can be more important than the ectopic origin itself.
therapies.title: Congenital anomalies of the coronary circulation

therapies.text: Left main from the right sinus passing between aorta and RV outflow tract. The source identifies the left main or major left branch passing between the aorta and RV outflow tract as particularly concerning; ostial shape and exercise also affect risk.
therapies.title: Congenital anomalies of the coronary circulation

therapies.text: Absence of a common left main trunk, generally functionally benign. Separate patent LAD and circumflex origins are different from a blind or imperforate left main origin.
therapies.title: Congenital anomalies of the coronary circulation

therapies.text: It may create major surgical risk despite little baseline physiologic effect. A coronary crossing the outflow tract can be endangered during intervention even when its resting physiologic effect is small.
therapies.title: Congenital anomalies of the coronary circulation

therapies.text: Adequate channels from a normally arising right coronary artery. Survival depends on adequate connections from the right coronary artery to the distal left system; presentation can span infancy to adulthood.
therapies.title: Congenital anomalies of the coronary circulation

cards.q: Why can a congenital cardiac malformation first become clinically apparent in adulthood?
cards.a: Congenital anatomy can acquire changing physiologic expression over time. A congenital malformation may evolve during gestation and extrauterine life; a bicuspid valve can become stenotic decades after birth.

cards.q: Why does a normal gross cardiac structure not exclude a congenital functional cardiac disorder?
cards.a: Congenital functional abnormalities can exist without a gross structural defect. The source includes congenital complete heart block among functionally significant conditions that need not be gross structural defects.

cards.q: How does the fall in pulmonary vascular resistance after birth affect the interpretation of congenital circulation?
cards.a: Lung expansion and falling pulmonary vascular resistance redistribute flow. Lung expansion, rising oxygen tension, reduced pulmonary resistance and elimination of the placental circulation substantially alter cardiovascular physiology.

cards.q: How should advanced imaging relate to the history, examination, ECG and chest radiograph?
cards.a: Integrate the imaging with prior clinical observations and predicted physiology. The diagnostic approach synthesizes history, examination, ECG, radiography and advanced imaging into a coherent anatomic–physiologic explanation.

cards.q: Why may examination reasonably precede completion of the history in an irritable infant?
cards.a: Examine while calm and integrate the history and other findings afterward. The depth and synthesis of analysis matter more than a rigid order; examining an infant during a calm interval may improve the assessment.

cards.q: What are the five cornerstone questions used to organize congenital cardiac recognition?
cards.a: Ask about cyanosis, increased or decreased pulmonary arterial flow, the side from which the malformation originates, the dominant ventricle, and pulmonary hypertension. These organize reasoning rather than replace anatomic confirmation.

cards.q: Which pattern is characteristic of a Still murmur?
cards.a: A Still murmur. The typical Still murmur is vibratory or buzzing, midsystolic and most prominent between the apex and lower left sternal edge in the supine child.

cards.q: Where are transient neonatal branch pulmonary artery systolic murmurs typically distributed?
cards.a: Transient disparity between the pulmonary trunk and its branch sizes. The neonatal pulmonary trunk–branch size disparity and branch geometry can produce widely transmitted systolic turbulence; the murmur alone does not distinguish transient physiology from fixed branch stenosis.

cards.q: How can positional behavior support recognition of a venous hum?
cards.a: A cervical venous hum. Recumbency, neutral neck position and reduced jugular flow can diminish or abolish the venous hum.

cards.q: What response to shoulder hyperextension supports a supraclavicular arterial systolic murmur?
cards.a: Flow vibrations near the origins of the major brachiocephalic arteries. The supraclavicular arterial murmur is systolic, maximal above the clavicles and may diminish or disappear with shoulder hyperextension.

cards.category: Association is not a settled mechanism
cards.q: Why does finding a ventricular band not establish the cause of every Still murmur?
cards.a: Band prevalence persists across ages while Still murmur prevalence falls toward adolescence. The mismatch between age-related murmur prevalence and band prevalence, and the source’s explicit uncertainty, prevent treating the association as a settled universal mechanism.

cards.q: What qualification is needed for the statement that functional murmurs are not solely diastolic?
cards.a: The source describes a rare transient neonatal ductal diastolic murmur in the first few days of life. Persistent or otherwise unexplained diastolic sounds should not be dismissed by applying an innocent-murmur label.

cards.q: What is meant by cardiac displacement?
cards.a: Secondary cardiac displacement. Cardiac displacement is a secondary shift in intrathoracic position, such as one produced by diaphragmatic eventration.

cards.q: What is the purpose of sequential segmental cardiac analysis?
cards.a: Identify the atria, valves, ventricles and arterial connections systematically. The source describes systematic attention to morphology, atrioventricular connections, ventriculoarterial connections and great-artery relationships.
