cards.q: Which combined findings support mirror-image situs inversus with dextrocardia?
cards.a: Situs inversus with dextrocardia. The described heart and abdominal viscera are in the mirror-image positions of the usual arrangement.

cards.category: The effect of two discordant connections
cards.q: Why can double discordance produce a circulation in series?
cards.a: Two discordant connections restore the appropriate destinations of blood. Atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial discordance can together produce physiologic correction of blood-flow destinations.

cards.q: What defines right isomerism in the structures described by the source?
cards.a: Right isomerism. Right isomerism describes bilateral morphologically right characteristics in structures normally different on the two sides.

cards.q: Why should ventricular identity not be assigned from left or right location alone?
cards.a: Position can be inverted or malposed. Identify morphologic components and their atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial connections before describing the resulting circulation.

cards.q: How can maternal autoantibodies cause congenital complete heart block?
cards.a: Transplacental transfer of maternal IgG with injury to fetal conduction tissue. The source describes passive autoimmunity involving maternal IgG antibodies, including Ro/SSA and La/SSB associations; maternal lupus can become apparent only later.

cards.q: Which ECG relationship establishes complete atrioventricular dissociation?
cards.a: Atrial and ventricular activation are independent. In complete heart block, P waves and QRS complexes occur independently, rather than maintaining a fixed conducted relationship.

cards.q: Why do intermittent cannon A waves occur in complete heart block?
cards.a: Right atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve. Independent atrial and ventricular activity can bring atrial contraction against the closed tricuspid valve, abruptly amplifying the venous A wave.

cards.q: Why can the first heart sound vary from beat to beat during complete heart block?
cards.a: The changing atrial–ventricular timing alters valve position at ventricular systole. Because atria and ventricles beat independently, the PR relationship changes and first-sound intensity can vary widely.

cards.category: Normal radiography does not exclude block
cards.q: Can a normal-looking chest radiograph rule out congenital complete heart block?
cards.a: Assess the atrial–ventricular relationship on a standard ECG. The radiographic appearance can be normal; the source emphasizes the standard ECG for establishing complete heart block.

cards.q: Why are narrow QRS complexes common in isolated congenital complete heart block?
cards.a: The usual subsidiary pacemaker is above the bifurcation of the His bundle, preserving a normal ventricular activation sequence. The source also discusses exceptions, so QRS width is interpreted with the whole ECG.

cards.q: What structure may herniate through a partial left pericardial defect and alter the left cardiac border?
cards.a: Herniation of the left atrial appendage through a partial left pericardial defect. Partial absence of the left pericardium may permit left atrial appendage herniation, producing the described convex left-border shadow.

cards.q: Which combination suggests complete congenital pericardial absence?
cards.a: Loss of normal pericardial restraint. Complete absence can produce striking cardiac mobility, leftward/posterior displacement and interposed lung tissue.

cards.q: Which modalities establish the pericardial anatomy when echocardiography raises suspicion?
cards.a: Thoracic CT or cardiac MRI. The source identifies CT and MRI as definitive modalities; echocardiography may suggest complete absence and identify coexisting defects.

cards.q: What is a typical chest-radiograph appearance of a congenital pericardial cyst?
cards.a: A congenital pericardial cyst. A congenital pericardial cyst typically forms a smooth homogeneous density at the right cardiophrenic angle.

cards.q: Why can complete pericardial absence affect right-sided chamber dimensions disproportionately?
cards.a: Reduced pericardial restraint particularly affects the relatively thin-walled right-sided chambers. Loss of normal pericardial constraint particularly affects the right ventricle and right atrium and can alter systemic venous return and septal motion.

cards.q: How does cardiac motion help distinguish partial from complete pericardial absence in this source?
cards.a: Partial left absence may leave overall position and movement normal while producing focal appendage herniation. Complete absence can permit striking mobility and leftward/posterior displacement. Confirm anatomy with appropriate imaging.

cards.q: Which two discordances produce the physiologically corrected circulation?
cards.a: Atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial discordance. Two discordant junctions place systemic venous blood in the pulmonary circuit and pulmonary venous blood in the systemic circuit, so the circulations are in series.

cards.q: Which ventricular morphology supports the systemic circulation in the typical double-discordant arrangement?
cards.a: The systemic morphologic right ventricle must sustain a workload for which its usual geometry and blood supply are not designed. The systemic right ventricle retains right-ventricular geometry and a morphologically right coronary supply despite systemic loading.

cards.q: Which morphologic valve can have an Ebstein-like malformation in the left atrioventricular position?
cards.a: Morphologic tricuspid valve. The inverted left atrioventricular valve is morphologically tricuspid; Ebstein-like abnormalities and age-related regurgitation are important.

cards.q: What change in the long penetrating atrioventricular bundle can cause progressive block?
cards.a: Replacement of conduction fibers by fibrous tissue in the long penetrating bundle. Fibrous replacement in the long penetrating bundle contributes to age-related atrioventricular block; defects may occur at several conduction levels.

cards.q: What precordial Q-wave pattern follows reversed septal depolarization?
cards.a: Q waves in right precordial leads with absent left precordial Q waves. Inverted bundle branches activate the septum from right to left, reversing the usual precordial septal Q-wave pattern.

cards.q: Which echocardiographic features identify a morphologic right ventricle rather than relying on its side of the chest?
cards.a: Coarse trabeculation, a moderator band, relatively distal atrioventricular valve insertion and tricuspid morphology help identify the morphologic right ventricle.

cards.q: What does an aortic ejection sound indicate about the level of obstruction?
cards.a: A mobile stenotic aortic valve. The sound arises from abrupt movement of a mobile doming valve and identifies valvar level rather than degree.

cards.category: A quiet murmur in ventricular failure
cards.q: How can left ventricular failure alter an aortic stenosis murmur?
cards.a: Reduced murmur intensity does not establish reduced obstruction. Aortic stenosis murmur intensity can decrease in left ventricular failure; loudness is not a stand-alone measure of obstruction.

cards.q: How can a bicuspid valve with a prominent false raphe be distinguished from a trileaflet valve?
cards.a: Image the open valve for two unequal doming leaflets and an elliptical orifice. Open-valve imaging reveals the bicuspid anatomy that can be obscured by a false raphe during closure.

cards.q: What arterial pulse pattern characterizes chronic severe aortic regurgitation?
cards.a: Rapid rise, wide pulse pressure and brisk collapse. Chronic severe regurgitation produces a rapid upstroke, wide pulse pressure, sometimes a bisferiens peak, and brisk collapse.

cards.q: Why can acute severe aortic regurgitation have a short soft diastolic murmur?
cards.a: Relatively low regurgitant flow velocity can make severe acute disease acoustically unimpressive. The source describes short, medium-pitched, disarmingly soft murmurs in acute severe regurgitation; chronic peripheral signs may be absent.

cards.q: What does echocardiography with continuous-wave Doppler add in congenital aortic stenosis?
cards.a: It defines level and morphology, estimates the transobstruction gradient and assesses ventricular dimensions and function rather than relying on murmur intensity alone.

cards.q: Which pulse comparison is useful for detecting coarctation?
cards.a: Compare upper-extremity and femoral pulses and blood pressures. Upper–lower extremity pulse and pressure differences are hallmarks; brachial–femoral comparison is particularly practical in infants.

cards.q: How does the proximal aorta contribute to coarctation-associated systolic hypertension?
cards.a: A stiff, poorly distensible precoarctation aorta. Increased collagen and reduced smooth muscle stiffen the proximal aorta, contributing to systolic hypertension and baroreceptor resetting.

cards.q: Why does absent rib notching not exclude coarctation in infancy?
cards.a: Notching usually develops later through enlarged posterior intercostal collateral arteries. Collateral posterior intercostal arteries produce notching, which seldom appears before age six years.

cards.q: When can a neonate with severe coarctation become acutely symptomatic?
cards.a: Closure of the ductus arteriosus. The source specifically associates acute neonatal symptoms in severe coarctation with ductal closure.

cards.q: How can femoral pulses be maintained initially in an infant with interrupted aortic arch?
cards.a: Pulmonary trunk through a patent ductus into the descending aorta. Pulmonary trunk–ductus–descending aortic continuity can supply the lower body; diminishing femoral pulses can signal ductal constriction.

cards.q: Where may a coarctation murmur be heard in an infant when anterior auscultation is unrevealing?
cards.a: Over the posterior thoracic spine near the coarctation; murmurs may diminish or disappear with heart failure.

cards.q: What defines a parachute mitral valve?
cards.a: Parachute mitral valve. A single papillary muscle receiving all chordae defines the parachute arrangement and can restrict interchordal flow.

cards.q: Which obstructive lesions form the classic Shone complex?
cards.a: Supravalvular mitral ring, parachute mitral valve, subaortic stenosis and coarctation. The classic four lesions are left-sided inflow/outflow obstructions; not all need be present or functionally significant.

cards.q: Why may congenital mitral stenosis lack a loud S1 and opening snap?
cards.a: The abnormal leaflet apparatus may not make the brisk opening and closing movements required for those sounds. The characteristic brisk motion of a mobile anterior leaflet is not a feature of the congenital lesion described.

cards.q: Where is the typical cor-triatriatum membrane relative to the left atrial appendage?
cards.a: Cor triatriatum. A membrane proximal to the appendage and valve distinguishes typical cor triatriatum from a supravalvular ring.

cards.q: Why can congenital pulmonary vein stenosis cause nonuniform pulmonary congestion without left atrial enlargement?
cards.a: Unequal stenosis of individual pulmonary veins proximal to the left atrium. Individual veins can have different severities of narrowing, producing regional congestion while the downstream left atrium remains normal-sized.

cards.q: How does the partition in typical cor triatriatum divide the left atrium?
cards.a: A proximal high-pressure accessory chamber receives the pulmonary veins; the distal chamber contains the left atrial appendage and fossa ovalis.

cards.q: What morphologic features characterize a dysplastic stenotic pulmonary valve?
cards.a: Dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis. Dysplastic pulmonary stenosis has thickened separate poorly mobile leaflets without commissural fusion.

cards.q: How does a typical mobile pulmonary-valve ejection sound change with inspiration?
cards.a: Reduced additional cephalad movement of a mobile pulmonary valve during ventricular contraction. Inspiration prepositions the mobile valve cephalad through increased right atrial contraction, reducing further excursion and the ejection sound.

cards.category: Critical obstruction with a soft murmur
cards.q: Can pinpoint neonatal pulmonary stenosis produce a soft murmur?
cards.a: Pinpoint pulmonary stenosis can have a deceptively soft murmur. The source emphasizes that pinpoint neonatal stenosis may sound disarmingly soft despite severe obstruction.

cards.category: Branch stenosis and the second sound
cards.q: Why can the pulmonary component of S2 remain normal in branch pulmonary artery stenosis?
cards.a: The central pulmonary diastolic pressure can remain normal or nearly normal at valve closure. Branch stenosis can raise central systolic pressure while pressure falls to near-normal diastolic levels, so valve closure need not be accentuated.

cards.q: What diastolic murmur pattern is described in isolated low-pressure congenital pulmonary regurgitation?
cards.a: Short delayed low-to-medium-frequency crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the upper left sternal border. The source describes a distinctive short delayed low-to-medium-frequency diastolic murmur, sometimes louder with inspiration.

cards.q: How does a double-chambered right ventricle create obstruction?
cards.a: Obstructing intracavitary muscle bundles divide the right ventricle into a high-pressure inlet portion and a lower-pressure outlet portion; a ventricular septal defect commonly coexists.

cards.q: What is the atrialized right ventricle in Ebstein anatomy?
cards.a: The inlet right ventricle between the anatomic annulus and displaced functional valve. Apical displacement atrializes the proximal inlet right ventricle while the trabecular and outlet portions form the functional right ventricle.

cards.q: Why may prominent systolic jugular V waves be absent despite severe Ebstein-related regurgitation?
cards.a: A large compliant right atrium and toneless atrialized ventricle damp low-pressure regurgitant flow. Commodious right-sided chambers and low-pressure hypokinetic regurgitation can damp the expected jugular signs.

cards.q: How can neonatal cyanosis improve and recur years later in Ebstein anomaly?
cards.a: A neonatal right-to-left atrial shunt can diminish as pulmonary resistance falls and reappear when abnormal right ventricular filling pressure rises. The source describes this uncommon course through changing right-sided filling conditions and interatrial shunting.

cards.q: Which ECG finding supports preexcitation rather than short PR alone?
cards.a: Preexcitation. Early delta-wave inscription supports preexcitation; a short PR interval alone can occasionally occur without a delta wave or tachycardia history.

cards.q: What should echocardiography assess beyond displaced tricuspid leaflet anatomy?
cards.a: Identify a PFO or secundum defect and determine interatrial shunt direction. Color flow imaging and Doppler identify the atrial pathway and whether right-to-left shunting coexists.

cards.q: What distinctive electrical-mechanical combination characterizes the atrialized right ventricle?
cards.a: It generates a ventricular intracavitary electrogram but an atrial-type pressure pulse, unlike the functional right ventricle.

cards.q: What mainly determines shunt volume across a nonrestrictive atrial septal defect?
cards.a: Relative compliance of the two ventricles. With little atrial pressure difference, preferential filling of the more compliant right ventricle produces the usual left-to-right shunt.

cards.q: Where does the typical midsystolic murmur of a nonrestrictive atrial septal defect originate?
cards.a: Increased flow through the pulmonary outflow and pulmonary trunk. The systolic murmur reflects augmented pulmonary flow, not a high-velocity jet across the nonrestrictive atrial communication.

cards.q: What does fixed splitting mean?
cards.a: Wide fixed splitting. Fixed denotes unchanged separation with respiration; persistent splitting remains audible but varies in width.

cards.q: What imaging-clinical combination supports obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous connection?
cards.a: Obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous connection. Obstructed anomalous venous return can produce severe neonatal hypoxemia and congestion with an unimpressive heart size and attenuated flow murmur.

cards.q: What leaflet arrangement permits both atrial and ventricular shunting in a complete common atrioventricular canal?
cards.a: Communication at both atrial and ventricular levels. Free-floating bridging leaflets permit both atrial and ventricular components of the complete canal.

cards.q: How does persistent PFO differ from a true secundum tissue defect?
cards.a: A PFO retains a valve at the fossa ovalis that has not fused completely; a true secundum defect represents deficient septal tissue rather than simply persistence of the flap-valve channel.

cards.q: What typical combination accompanies severe pulmonary valve stenosis and a right-to-left atrial shunt?
cards.a: Patent foramen ovale. Severe pulmonary stenosis with right-to-left shunting most often uses a patent foramen ovale; a nonrestrictive secundum defect more often accompanies mild-to-moderate stenosis and left-to-right flow.

cards.q: How can severe pulmonary stenosis generate a presystolic right-to-left atrial shunt?
cards.a: High right atrial pressure stretches the foramen and drives blood toward the left atrium. Forceful atrial contraction raises right atrial pressure, increases PFO patency and can generate a presystolic right-to-left shunt.

cards.q: How does warmth help distinguish peripheral low-flow cyanosis from a central shunt contribution?
cards.a: A low-skin-flow peripheral component has improved; central shunt cyanosis must still be assessed. Warmth improves skin blood flow and can diminish peripheral cyanosis while making any persistent central component easier to recognize.

cards.q: What auscultatory additions suggest pulmonary valve stenosis in a nonrestrictive atrial septal defect?
cards.a: Coexisting mobile pulmonary valve stenosis. The combination adds valvar ejection sound, a longer louder stenotic murmur and further delay and softening of P2 to the atrial-shunt findings.

cards.q: Which imaging tools establish the valve obstruction and atrial shunt direction?
cards.a: Doppler for the obstructive gradient and color flow for the interatrial shunt. Imaging identifies the valve and interatrial pathway; Doppler assesses the gradient and color flow confirms shunt direction.

cards.q: Why does raised right atrial pressure with an atrial communication increase paradoxical embolic risk?
cards.a: It can promote right-to-left passage across a PFO or atrial defect, allowing systemic venous embolic material access to the arterial circulation.

cards.q: What makes a ventricular septal defect restrictive?
cards.a: Restrictive defect. Restriction at the defect limits pressure transmission and shunt flow, leaving a systolic pressure difference.

cards.q: Why can a sizable ventricular left-to-right shunt become symptomatic after the newborn period?
cards.a: Falling pulmonary vascular resistance increases left-to-right flow. The neonatal fall in pulmonary resistance permits a larger shunt and pulmonary venous return, imposing left ventricular volume load.

cards.q: How can pulmonary vascular disease reverse a nonrestrictive ventricular shunt?
cards.a: Right-to-left shunting from pulmonary vascular disease. With equal ventricular systolic pressures, relative vascular resistances govern flow; suprasystemic pulmonary resistance favors reversal.

cards.q: Why may the murmur shorten and soften as pulmonary vascular resistance rises?
cards.a: Reduced left-to-right flow can reflect worsening pulmonary vascular disease. As pulmonary resistance approaches systemic, the left-to-right murmur can shorten, soften and eventually disappear with reversal.

cards.q: Which valve abnormality should be sought when a ventricular defect is accompanied by aortic regurgitation?
cards.a: Aortic cusp prolapse and regurgitation. Perimembranous and subarterial defects can be associated with aortic cusp prolapse; regurgitant volume can explain disproportionate left ventricular enlargement.

cards.q: How can perimembranous ventricular defects close spontaneously?
cards.a: Adherence of septal tricuspid leaflet tissue to the defect margins is a common mechanism and can be associated with a membranous septal aneurysm.

cards.q: Which malalignment links the principal anatomy of tetralogy of Fallot?
cards.a: Anterior and cephalad deviation of the infundibular septum. Outlet septal malalignment creates the ventricular defect, narrows right ventricular outflow and contributes to aortic override.

cards.q: What chiefly determines shunt direction in classic tetralogy with a nonrestrictive defect?
cards.a: More right-to-left flow into the aorta and less pulmonary flow. Relative outflow and systemic resistances determine the balance; severe outflow obstruction diverts blood toward the aorta.

cards.q: Why can the pulmonary stenotic murmur soften during a hypoxic spell?
cards.a: A sharp decline in forward pulmonary blood flow. Less blood traverses the stenotic pulmonary outflow, so the murmur shortens and softens despite worsening hypoxemia.

cards.q: How can squatting improve oxygenation in an unrepaired tetralogy circulation?
cards.a: Increased systemic resistance and reduced return of desaturated leg blood. Squatting can redirect right ventricular flow toward the lungs and curtail desaturated lower-extremity venous return.

cards.q: Why is right ventricular systolic pressure usually systemic in classic tetralogy?
cards.a: The ventricle can decompress through the communication into the systemic outlet. The nonrestrictive defect imposes a systemic pressure ceiling; partial occlusion or true restriction can remove that protection.

cards.q: Why can pulmonary atresia in this anatomy coexist with only mild cyanosis?
cards.a: Abundant systemic-to-pulmonary collateral flow can supply effective pulmonary gas exchange despite absent forward right ventricular pulmonary flow.

cards.q: How does this source pragmatically define double outlet right ventricle?
cards.a: Double outlet right ventricle. The chapter uses ventricular support of most of both arterial valves as its pragmatic definition while acknowledging classification debates.

cards.q: Where does left ventricular blood preferentially stream with a subpulmonary ventricular communication?
cards.a: Left ventricular blood preferentially enters the pulmonary trunk. A subpulmonary communication directs left ventricular output toward the pulmonary outlet, creating a transposition-like physiology.

cards.q: What physiology can subaortic double outlet right ventricle without pulmonary stenosis resemble?
cards.a: A large ventricular left-to-right shunt with increased pulmonary flow. Low pulmonary resistance permits increased pulmonary flow and left ventricular volume overload, resembling a large isolated ventricular defect.

cards.q: How does pulmonary stenosis change subaortic double outlet physiology?
cards.a: Less pulmonary flow and more blood directed to the aorta. Obstruction diverts both ventricular streams away from the pulmonary outlet and toward the aorta, producing a tetralogy-like pattern.

cards.q: Why can a restrictive ventricular communication be hazardous in double outlet right ventricle?
cards.a: Obstruction to left ventricular egress and subaortic flow. The communication is an essential left ventricular exit; restriction can act as subaortic stenosis rather than a uniformly favorable reduction in shunt.

cards.q: What does atrioventricular valve straddling mean?
cards.a: Chordal attachments insert on both sides of the ventricular septum; this differs from overriding, which describes biventricular commitment of the valve annulus.

cards.q: Where are the usual aortic and pulmonary openings of a patent ductus?
cards.a: Patent ductus arteriosus. The normal ductal insertion is near the left pulmonary artery, with its aortic end distal to the left subclavian artery.

cards.q: How does a left-to-right ductal shunt load the left ventricle?
cards.a: Increased pulmonary venous return imposes left ventricular volume load. Pulmonary recirculation returns to the left atrium and ventricle, increasing left-heart volume load.

cards.q: How does the classic uncomplicated ductal murmur relate to the second sound?
cards.a: Classic continuous ductal murmur. The classic ductal sound envelops the second heart sound with continuous systolic-to-diastolic flow.

cards.q: Why can a reversed ductal shunt cause cyanotic toes with a pink right hand?
cards.a: Pulmonary arterial blood entering the descending aorta through a ductus distal to the right-arm supply. The ductal entry usually delivers desaturated blood to the lower body after the proximal arch vessels have branched.

cards.q: Why does reversed flow through an aortopulmonary window usually lack differential cyanosis?
cards.a: Desaturated blood enters proximal to systemic arch distribution. A window delivers blood into the ascending aorta, unlike the usual distal ductal insertion.

cards.q: Why can a clinically silent ductus remain patent?
cards.a: Jet direction and pressure-flow conditions can prevent an audible murmur; Doppler imaging can identify patency despite absent auscultatory signs.

cards.q: Why can ischemia emerge after the neonatal fall in pulmonary pressure?
cards.a: Falling pulmonary pressure reduces antegrade perfusion through the anomalous artery. Initially high pulmonary pressure can support antegrade flow. Its postnatal fall reduces that supply unless intercoronary perfusion becomes adequate.

cards.q: How can intercoronary collateral flow both help and harm in pulmonary-origin left coronary anatomy?
cards.a: Collaterals restore some perfusion but also permit a low-resistance coronary steal. The collateral route can nourish myocardium while also bypassing capillaries toward a low-pressure pulmonary outlet.

cards.q: Why can anomalous left coronary origin cause mitral regurgitation?
cards.a: Ischemic papillary muscle dysfunction. Papillary muscle ischemia can impair mitral competence and add regurgitant volume to an already compromised ventricle.

cards.q: Which ECG pattern should raise suspicion for pulmonary-origin left coronary artery in a symptomatic infant?
cards.a: Anomalous left coronary artery from the pulmonary trunk. Deep narrow lateral q waves, often with left ventricular hypertrophy and a leftward axis, are a characteristic clue; early infant tracings can be less conspicuous.

cards.q: What imaging observation separates anomalous coronary origin from a coronary-to-pulmonary fistula?
cards.a: Define whether the left coronary arises from the pulmonary trunk or from its normal aortic sinus. An anomalous left coronary lacks its normal aortic origin; a coronary arterial fistula can have similar pulmonary flow while both coronary arteries retain aortic origins.

cards.q: Does asymptomatic survival to adulthood establish that a pulmonary-origin left coronary artery is benign?
cards.a: No. Adult presentations can include mitral regurgitation, ischemia, ventricular arrhythmia, cardiac arrest or sudden death despite little earlier symptom burden.

cards.q: What defines a typical congenital coronary arterial fistula?
cards.a: Congenital coronary arterial fistula. A fistulous branch provides an abnormal drainage route despite usually appropriate coronary origins.

cards.q: Why can a large coronary-to-right atrial fistula load both ventricles?
cards.a: Left-to-right recirculation with right and left ventricular volume loading. Blood enters the right atrium and traverses the right heart, lungs and left heart before returning to the aorta.

cards.q: How can a coronary fistula cause ischemia without a very large pulmonary shunt?
cards.a: Low-resistance runoff can divert coronary blood away from myocardium. Myocardial steal depends on the low-resistance alternative pathway and the coronary territory involved, not only total pulmonary shunt size.

cards.q: What chiefly determines where a coronary fistula murmur is loudest?
cards.a: The chamber or vessel receiving the fistula. The drainage site determines the intracardiac sound source and corresponding thoracic location.

cards.q: What murmur can a coronary-to-left ventricular fistula generate?
cards.a: Aortic-to-ventricular pressure difference favors diastolic fistulous flow. A coronary-to-left ventricular communication can produce an early diastolic murmur; systolic flow depends on the stoma and compression pattern.

cards.q: How does the feeding coronary artery often appear proximal to a fistula?
cards.a: It is often dilated, elongated and tortuous, while distal coronary branches may remain of normal caliber.

cards.q: Where does a noncoronary sinus aneurysm most often rupture?
cards.a: Right atrium. The noncoronary sinus is anatomically related to the right atrium; right coronary sinus aneurysms commonly enter the right ventricle or sometimes the right atrium.

cards.q: Why can a sudden large sinus rupture cause rapid congestive failure?
cards.a: The heart has little time to adapt to the acute shunt volume burden. Size, rapidity and receiving chamber determine the burden; sudden substantial recirculation can overwhelm adaptation.

cards.q: What should a new continuous murmur with acute symptoms suggest in someone with a ventricular septal defect?
cards.a: Rupture of a coexisting sinus of Valsalva aneurysm. The source highlights this change as a clue to an aortic sinus aneurysm rupturing into the right side of the heart.

cards.q: How may a sinus rupture murmur differ from a classic ductal murmur?
cards.a: A ruptured aortic sinus communication is plausible. Sinus rupture murmurs can be continuous without the characteristic second-sound peak of the classic ductal murmur.

cards.q: How can an aortic sinus aneurysm cause atrioventricular block?
cards.a: Injury to the AV node or His bundle near the septal base. Ruptured or unruptured aneurysms penetrating the septal base can disrupt nearby conduction tissue.

cards.q: Can an unruptured sinus aneurysm produce a to-and-fro murmur?
cards.a: Yes. Flow into and out of the intact pouch can cause murmurs in both phases; color Doppler assessment is needed to distinguish this from an actual perforation.

cards.q: How does systemic venous blood reach the left heart in pulmonary atresia with an intact ventricular septum?
cards.a: Right-to-left flow through an interatrial communication. The interatrial communication is the right atrium’s exit to the left heart; its restriction can add to the circulatory problem.

cards.q: Why is ductal patency crucial in the usual unrepaired neonatal circulation?
cards.a: Effective pulmonary blood flow can cease. The ductus supplies the pulmonary circuit in the usual anatomy; systemic-to-pulmonary collaterals are generally inadequate.

cards.q: Does pulmonary atresia with an intact septum always imply a tiny right ventricle?
cards.a: Both patterns occur, and tricuspid competence helps explain their different appearances. The chapter describes a common small-ventricle pattern and a less common dilated pattern associated with an incompetent dysplastic or Ebstein-like valve.

cards.q: What makes some coronary circulations right ventricular dependent?
cards.a: High right ventricular systolic pressure drives retrograde coronary flow. When aortic access is obstructed, myocardial perfusion can depend on suprasystemic right ventricular pressure supplying the coronary bed.

cards.q: Can a small thick-walled right ventricle lack prominent ECG evidence of RV hypertrophy?
cards.a: The small cavity can generate little right ventricular electrical amplitude despite its thick wall. The source describes absent prominent RV hypertrophy voltage in the small-ventricle pattern; chamber geometry and cavity size matter.

cards.q: What does functional pulmonary atresia mean in the source’s distinction?
cards.a: A dilated mechanically inadequate right ventricle cannot generate enough pressure to open a stenotic but anatomically nonatretic pulmonary valve, often with severe tricuspid regurgitation.

cards.q: How does systemic venous blood reach the ventricle in tricuspid atresia?
cards.a: Right-to-left flow across an interatrial communication. Systemic venous blood must cross from right atrium to left atrium and pass through the patent left AV valve.

cards.q: Why can spontaneous VSD closure be harmful in tricuspid atresia with normally related great arteries?
cards.a: Increasing subpulmonary obstruction limits lung flow. With normally related arteries, the ventricular communication provides access to the pulmonary circuit; narrowing can produce acquired pulmonary atresia.

cards.q: What can a restrictive VSD obstruct when tricuspid atresia is accompanied by transposed great arteries?
cards.a: Subaortic obstruction to systemic output. In this arrangement left ventricular blood must traverse the defect to reach the transposed aorta; restriction creates subaortic stenosis.

cards.q: What ECG pattern supports the common non-transposed form with a restrictive ventricular defect?
cards.a: Left-axis deviation with adult-like precordial progression and right atrial P waves. The source summary describes left-axis deviation, counterclockwise depolarization, adult precordial progression and right atrial P waves in this common arrangement.

cards.q: What does echocardiography with color flow and Doppler establish in tricuspid atresia?
cards.a: Echocardiography with color flow and Doppler. Echo identifies the echodense absent connection, chamber sizes, great arterial relationships and shunt or obstruction physiology.

cards.q: Why can mild cyanosis coexist with heart failure in tricuspid atresia?
cards.a: A nonrestrictive ventricular defect and low pulmonary vascular resistance can cause excessive pulmonary flow and left ventricular volume overload, reducing cyanosis at the price of heart failure.

cards.q: What anatomic connection defines a morphologic univentricular heart?
cards.a: A morphologically defined single ventricular connection. The chapter defines the anatomy by atrial and AV connections to one main ventricular chamber, distinguishing it from other functionally single-ventricle categories.

cards.q: How does pulmonary flow influence presentation in a single-ventricle heart?
cards.a: Excess pulmonary flow with ventricular volume overload. Excess pulmonary flow produces heart failure and poor growth despite relatively mild cyanosis.

cards.q: Can systemic and pulmonary venous streams remain partly separate within a single ventricle?
cards.a: Preferential streaming can direct oxygenated blood toward the aorta. The source describes partial stream separation influenced by outlet arrangement and pulmonary resistance.

cards.q: Why can progressive restriction of the outlet foramen worsen single-left-ventricle physiology?
cards.a: Subaortic obstruction with diversion toward the pulmonary circuit and greater volume burden. Restriction creates subaortic stenosis and may augment already excessive pulmonary flow and ventricular volume overload.

cards.q: Why can a pulmonary stenotic murmur shorten and soften as obstruction worsens in a single-ventricle heart?
cards.a: Less blood crosses the increasingly obstructed pulmonary outlet. As stenosis increases, more flow is diverted to the systemic outlet and less traverses the pulmonary obstruction, reducing its murmur.

cards.q: What associated structure should be assessed when subaortic stenosis has existed from infancy in a single-left-ventricle heart?
cards.a: The aortic arch should be assessed for coarctation or hypoplasia using appropriate imaging and Doppler, because these may accompany a restrictive systemic outlet.

cards.q: Which atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial connections define complete transposition?
cards.a: AV concordance with ventriculoarterial discordance and parallel circuits. Complete transposition combines AV concordance and ventriculoarterial discordance, creating parallel systemic and pulmonary recirculation.

cards.q: Why can increasing pulmonary flow fail to correct systemic hypoxemia when the atrial communication is restrictive?
cards.a: Oxygenated blood recirculates through the pulmonary circuit instead of adequately entering systemic flow. An adequate communication permits exchange between the circuits; a restrictive atrial route can leave oxygenated blood trapped in pulmonary recirculation.

cards.q: Can an early neonatal ECG be normal in complete transposition?
cards.a: A normal early ECG does not exclude the abnormal arterial connections. The chapter explicitly describes a potentially normal ECG in the first days; structural assessment remains essential.

cards.q: What can cause reversed differential cyanosis in complete transposition with a large ductus and pulmonary vascular disease?
cards.a: More oxygenated pulmonary arterial blood enters the descending aorta beyond the left subclavian artery. Oxygenated pulmonary arterial blood can pass through the ductus to the lower body, producing less cyanotic feet.

cards.q: What produces the characteristic egg-like cardiac silhouette in complete transposition with increased pulmonary flow?
cards.a: A prominent right atrium and convex enlarged left ventricle shape the silhouette. The right atrium forms the blunter right border and the enlarged left ventricle the convex left border; arterial arrangement contributes to the narrow pedicle.

cards.q: Why is coronary anatomy important even if it does not determine the initial physiology of complete transposition?
cards.a: The origins and proximal courses are anatomically pivotal for an arterial switch operation; they must be defined rather than assumed from the usual pattern.

cards.q: Which arterial beds arise from the common trunk?
cards.a: Truncus arteriosus. A single great artery and single semilunar valve supply the three circulations.

cards.q: How does type 1 truncus differ from a pattern with separate pulmonary branch ostia?
cards.a: Type 1 truncus. Type 1 has a short main pulmonary artery from the trunk; separate branch ostia constitute the other grouped pattern.

cards.q: Why can cyanosis diminish while heart failure worsens in an infant with truncus arteriosus?
cards.a: Falling pulmonary resistance increases lung flow and ventricular volume load. More pulmonary flow improves systemic oxygenation but imposes volume overload and may cause severe heart failure.

cards.q: Why can truncal valve regurgitation produce biventricular failure?
cards.a: Regurgitant flow is received by both ventricles and adds to their burden. The biventricular truncus permits regurgitant volume to load both ventricles, adding to existing hemodynamic stress.

cards.q: What associated syndrome should be considered with truncus, hypocalcemia and deficient cellular immunity?
cards.a: DiGeorge syndrome. The chapter describes DiGeorge-related thymic and parathyroid deficiency with truncus arteriosus.

cards.q: What imaging observations define truncal valve dysfunction?
cards.a: Color flow imaging assesses regurgitation, and continuous-wave Doppler assesses stenosis, alongside valve morphology and the pulmonary branching anatomy.

cards.q: What is the usual isolated physiologic effect of a left SVC draining through the coronary sinus to the right atrium?
cards.a: The route is usually physiologically harmless despite coronary sinus dilation. Blood still reaches the right atrium through the coronary sinus, so an isolated connection need not create a physiologic derangement.

cards.q: How can a left SVC-to-left atrial connection coexist with absent cyanosis?
cards.a: Left atrium to left SVC, across the bridge and into the right SVC. A freely communicating bridge can permit left-to-right flow from left atrium through the venous pathway to right atrium, reversing the expected cyanotic pattern.

cards.q: What route is described in isolated IVC interruption with azygos continuation?
cards.a: Azygos continuation, which can be physiologically insignificant in isolation. The interrupted inferior caval flow continues through a dilated azygos system to the right SVC; isolated cases need not cause a shunt.

cards.q: What congenital venous connection should be considered with an unexpectedly dilated coronary sinus?
cards.a: Persistent left superior vena cava. An unexpectedly enlarged coronary sinus can be the clue to an unsuspected left SVC; color and contrast studies define the route.

cards.q: Why may a cyanotic patient with anomalous caval-to-left atrial drainage lack right ventricular hypertrophy?
cards.a: Right-heart flow is normal or reduced because some systemic venous blood bypasses it. Anomalous caval return bypasses the right heart, unlike lesions with major RV pressure or volume overload.

cards.q: What neurologic complications can occur despite few symptoms in isolated caval drainage to the left atrium?
cards.a: Paradoxical embolism and brain abscess have been reported; modest hemodynamic burden does not eliminate complications of bypassing the pulmonary circulation.

cards.q: Why can a pulmonary arteriovenous fistula cause cyanosis without major ventricular volume overload?
cards.a: Blood bypasses gas exchange while flow through uninvolved lung may fall reciprocally. The right-to-left intrapulmonary route bypasses the capillary bed; redistribution can limit the net increase in ventricular flow.

cards.q: What inherited disorder links recurrent epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectases and pulmonary AV malformations?
cards.a: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia. The source describes an autosomal dominant vasculopathy with mucocutaneous bleeding and visceral arteriovenous malformations.

cards.q: Why should auscultation extend beyond the precordium when a pulmonary AV fistula is suspected?
cards.a: A peripheral pulmonary fistula can generate a localized flow murmur. Peripheral fistulae transmit sounds to the overlying chest wall; inspiratory flow and reduced compression may increase audibility.

cards.q: What does delayed left atrial contrast after a venous bubble injection usually suggest in this source?
cards.a: A pulmonary right-to-left shunt. The chapter describes delayed appearance beyond three cycles as usually indicating pulmonary shunting; the timing is a clue interpreted with anatomy.

cards.q: What important neurologic risks accompany pulmonary AV fistulae?
cards.a: Paradoxical embolism, stroke and brain abscess. The shunt bypasses the pulmonary filter; the source highlights embolic events and brain abscess.

cards.q: What radiographic finding helps identify a pulmonary fistula rather than a nonspecific lung nodule?
cards.a: A round or lobulated intrapulmonary density may have vascular shadows linking it to the hilum, representing afferent and efferent channels; small diffuse lesions may be poorly defined.

cards.q: How is the systemic circulation supplied in the aortic-atresia form of hypoplastic left heart?
cards.a: Right ventricle through pulmonary trunk, ductus and descending aorta. The pulmonary artery/ductus/descending aortic continuity provides systemic flow; retrograde flow supplies the small ascending aorta and coronary origins.

cards.q: Why is ductal constriction dangerous in aortic-atresia hypoplastic left heart?
cards.a: Reduced systemic and retrograde coronary perfusion impairs output and RV function. The ductus supports systemic and coronary supply; constriction compromises both and can worsen the sole pumping ventricle.

cards.q: Why can falling pulmonary resistance produce a shock-like state despite relatively high oxygen saturation?
cards.a: Flow is preferentially diverted to the lungs at the expense of systemic output. The right ventricle supplies both beds; increasing lung flow can improve mixing saturation while reducing systemic blood flow.

cards.q: Can hypoplastic left heart present with little or no murmur?
cards.a: A severe ductal-dependent left-heart lesion remains possible. The source emphasizes unimpressive auscultation despite dramatic illness; aortic atresia leaves a single pulmonary closure sound.

cards.q: Why does restrictive left atrial egress matter in hypoplastic left heart?
cards.a: Pulmonary venous return encounters an obstructed left atrium. The left atrium needs an alternative exit when mitral inflow is severely limited; atrial restriction compromises that exit and promotes congestion.

cards.q: Which echocardiographic findings should be assessed beyond left ventricular size?
cards.a: Define the aortic and mitral valves, atrial septum, ductal and arch pathways, retrograde ascending aortic flow, RV function and tricuspid competence.

cards.q: Why does an ectopic coronary origin require definition of the proximal course?
cards.a: Whether its course is anterior, retroaortic, interarterial or intramyocardial. The source emphasizes that the route relative to the great arteries can be more important than the ectopic origin itself.

cards.q: Which anomalous coronary arrangement carries the greatest risk in the chapter’s comparison?
cards.a: Left main from the right sinus passing between aorta and RV outflow tract. The source identifies the left main or major left branch passing between the aorta and RV outflow tract as particularly concerning; ostial shape and exercise also affect risk.

cards.q: How does absence of a left main trunk differ from left main ostial atresia?
cards.a: Absence of a common left main trunk, generally functionally benign. Separate patent LAD and circumflex origins are different from a blind or imperforate left main origin.

cards.q: Why is a coronary artery crossing the RV outflow tract important in tetralogy of Fallot?
cards.a: It may create major surgical risk despite little baseline physiologic effect. A coronary crossing the outflow tract can be endangered during intervention even when its resting physiologic effect is small.

cards.q: What permits survival when the left main coronary ostium is congenitally atretic?
cards.a: Adequate channels from a normally arising right coronary artery. Survival depends on adequate connections from the right coronary artery to the distal left system; presentation can span infancy to adulthood.

cards.q: Why is a single coronary artery not automatically equivalent to clinically dangerous coronary flow?
cards.a: A single ostium can give rise to normally formed and distributed branches; significance depends on factors including major branch hypoplasia and a potentially hazardous proximal course.

figures.caption: Fig. 2.9 (A) Illustration of Gallavardin dissociation of the two murmurs associated with fibrocalcific aortic stenosis of an inherently normal trileaflet aortic valve.75 The impure midsystolic murmur at the right base originates within the aortic root because of turbulence caused by the high velocity jet. The pure musical midsystolic murmur at the apex originates from periodic high frequency vibrations of the fibrocalcific aortic leaflets and radiates into the left ventricular cavity (LV). (B) Schematic illustrations that begin with the normal attachment of an aortic cusp to its sinus of Valsalva (normal). The initial alteration (mild) is a ridge-like fibrous thickening at the base of the aortic cusp as it inserts into its sinus. Calcium is subsequently deposited on the aortic surface of the leaflet (moderate), and ultimately extends to the free edge of the leaflet (severe), converting an inherently normal trileaflet valve into calcific aortic stenosis. (C) Schematic illustrations of a bicuspid aortic valve. The aortic cusp is thin and mobile yet domes during systole in a functionally normal bicuspid aortic valve (normal). The initial alteration (mild) is thickening of the leaflet tip with minimal restriction of mobility (mild). Calcium deposition occurs at the leaflet tip resulting in further restriction of mobility (moderate), eventually the calcification and fibrosis progresses proximally towards the cusp attachment to the sinus of Valsalva (severe) and the valve mobility is further reduced. The musical Gallavardin murmur does not occur in bicuspid aortic valve stenosis because leaflet mobility is not restricted to the same extent as in trileaflet aortic valve stenosis. Hence, there is an absence of the high-frequency fibrocalcific leaflet vibrations responsible for the musical quality of the murmur.

figures.caption: Fig. 6.1 (A) Gross specimen of congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries illustrating ventriculoarterial discordance. The pulmonary trunk originates from the morphologic left ventricle (LV) and the aorta (Ao) originates from the morphologic right ventricle (RV). (B and C) Illustrations of congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries for comparison with the normal heart. Congenitally corrected transposition is characterized by atrioventricular discordance and ventriculoarterial discordance. Blood from a morphologic right atrium (RA) traverses a morphologic mitral valve into a morphologic LV and then enters a pulmonary trunk (PT) that is rightward and posterior. Blood from a morphologic left atrium (LA) traverses a morphologic tricuspid valve into a morphologic RV and then enters an Ao that is leftward and anterior. The double discordance means that right atrial blood finds its way into the pulmonary artery and left atrial blood finds its way into the aorta. Anatomic transposition of the great arteries is physiologically corrected. The great arteries run parallel to each other and do not cross as in the normal heart. Coexisting anomalies include a malformed left atrioventricular valve, a ventricular septal defect, and pulmonary stenosis. (B) The normal heart is characterized by atrioventricular concordance, ventriculoarterial concordance, and a pulmonary artery that crosses anterior to the Ao.

Blood in the LV is thereafter ejected into a rightward PA. Oxygenated blood returning from the lungs via the pulmonary veins to the left atrium empties into a hypertrophied and dilated left sided systemic RV and is thereafter ejected into a levoposed Ao. (D) Sagittal view demonstrating the anterior and rightward location of the LV, the posterior and leftward location of the RV and ventriculoarterial discordance with the PA and Ao running parallel to one another.

figures.caption: Fig. 6.11 Collage of the catheterization findings and hemodynamic tracings of the 65-year-old male whose echocardiogram is displayed in Fig. 6.10. The findings are consistent with severe pulmonary stenosis and mild bidirectional shunting across a nonrestrictive ventricular septal defect. (A) Diagnostic cardiac catheterization data gathered while the patient was awake and breathing room air. The assumed pulmonary vein saturation is 97%. Using the Fick method, the calculated pulmonary blood flow is 3.5 L/min, the systemic blood flow is 3.4 L/min, and the effective pulmonary blood flow is 3.2 L/min. There is bidirectional shunting across the VSD with a net left to right shunt of 0.3 L/min and net right to left shunt of 0.2 L/min. (B) Simultaneous right pulmonary artery wedge pressure (blue) and systemic morphologic right ventricular pressure (red) demonstrate a mean gradient of 3 mm Hg and a calculated tricuspid valve area of 1.4 cm2, consistent with mild to moderate tricuspid stenosis. (C) Simultaneous subpulmonic morphologic left ventricular pressure and femoral artery pressure. Note that despite the high afterload faced by the morphologic left ventricle, the function remains well preserved and the filling pressure is low. (D) Pulmonary artery systolic pressure is nearly 100 mm Hg lower than the morphologic left ventricular systolic pressure, which is consistent with severe pulmonary valvular and subpulmonary stenosis. Despite all of the above abnormalities, this patient demonstrates a finely balanced circulation and hence the patient remains minimally symptomatic into the seventh decade. Ao, Aorta; LA, left atrium; LV, left ventricle; MV, mitral valve; PA, pulmonary artery; PS, pulmonic stenosis; RA, right atrium; RV, right ventricle; TS, tricuspid valve; VSD, ventricular septal defect.

figures.caption: Fig. 7.1 ​(A) Illustrations of the various types of aortic valve stenosis. Figure on the left illustrates three types of congenitally abnormal aortic valves. The upper drawing shows a unicuspid acommissural valve. The middle drawing shows a unicuspid unicommissural valve with an eccentric orifice. The lower group of four drawings shows a functionally normal bicuspid aortic valve (upper center), a fibrocalcific stenotic bicuspid aortic valve (center right), a bicuspid aortic that is inherently stenotic because the free edges are not longer than the annular diameter (center left), and a bicuspid aortic valve that is inherently stenotic because of failure of commissural separation (lower center). Illustrations on the right show a normal trileaflet aortic valve with equal cusps and equal commissures (center right). A congenitally hypoplastic trileaflet aortic valve (center left) is paired beside the normal trileaflet aortic valve (center left). Acquired aortic valve stenosis from fibrosis and calcification without commissural fusion (right lower) or from rheumatic fusion of commissures (upper). A dysplastic trileaflet valve is not shown. (B) Congenital aortic cuspal inequality as represented by Leonardo da Vinci circa 1513.1 His legend read: “Figures of the cusps (aorti) of the gateway which the left ventricle possesses when it closes itself.” On the left is a trileaflet aortic valve as seen from above. On the right is a closed trileaflet aortic valve as seen from below. (C) Dilation of the ascending aorta (AAo) above a congenitally bicuspid aortic valve (paired arrows) with a false raphe (curved arrow). (From Abbott M. Atlas of Congenital Cardiac Disease. Montreal: Osler Library, McGill University; 1936. Reproduced with permission.)

figures.caption: Fig. 8.7 ​A 55-year-old man with near interruption of the descending thoracic aorta. (A) CT angiogram, sagittal view demonstrating severe coarctation resulting in near interruption of the proximal descending aorta (*) distal to the take-off of the left subclavian artery. Note the web of large arterial collaterals (arrows) bypassing the coarctation and entering the descending thoracic aorta below the level of obstruction. (B) CT angiogram, coronal view of the chest wall just beneath the sternum demonstrating enlarged mammary arteries (arrows) serving as off-loading collaterals from the subclavian arteries above the level of coarctation. (C) Simultaneous ascending aortic and femoral arterial pressure tracings demonstrating a 50 mm Hg peak to peak systolic gradient; the mean arterial pressure difference, however, is less than 15 mm Hg. This is due to the extensive web of arterial collaterals as seen in panels A and B supplying a sufficient amount of arterial flow to the arterial system below the level of coarctation in order to maintain basal perfusion and avoid resting ischemia. However, this patient reports near disabling claudication of the lower limbs with ambulation up one flight of stairs which confirms that the collateral circulation is sufficient at rest or with minimal activity but cannot supply sufficient arterial blood flow to avoid ischemia with more strenuous lower extremity exercises.

figures.caption: Fig. 8.32 ​Illustration of the anatomic and circulatory derangements in the three types of complete aortic interruption. The descending aorta (DAo) is continuous with the pulmonary artery (PA) via a nonrestrictive patent ductus arteriosus (*). A large ventricular septal defect provides the left ventricle with access to the descending aorta via pulmonary trunk/ductus/descending aortic continuity. The red coloration denotes highly oxygenated blood that is being ejected from the left ventricle via the ascending aorta (Asc Ao). The blue coloration denotes deoxygenated/mixed-blood return ejected into the PA by both the right and left ventricles and then shunting right to left via a large patent ductus arteriosus (*). (A) Type A—Interruption of the distal arch is distal to the left subclavian artery (LSCA). (B) Type B—Interruption is the commonest type. The Asc Ao gives rise to the innominate artery (Innom A.) and to the left carotid artery (LCA). The interruption is in the mid-aortic arch. The LSCA arises distal to the obstruction. (C) Type C—The interruption is within the proximal arch distal to the Innom A.

figures.caption: Fig. 17.2 ​Illustrations of two major flow patterns in patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). (A) This illustration depicts a left-to-right shunt through a large tubular patent ductus in which pulmonary vascular resistance is lower than systemic vascular resistance. Shunt flow is from aorta (Ao) into the pulmonary artery (PA). The left atrium (LA) and left ventricle (LV) are enlarged due to the increased pulmonary blood flow and hence pulmonary venous return. The right ventricle (RV) is not enlarged. (B) This figure illustrates the long-term consequence of a large PDA and progressive increase in pulmonary arterial resistance to a suprasystemic level. Shunt flow is from PA into the Ao immediately distal to the left subclavian artery, and hence the lower body is cyanotic. The LA and LV are not enlarged, because the pulmonary venous return is limited by the severity of the pulmonary arterial disease. The RV is enlarged and hypertrophied.

figures.caption: Fig. 17.11 ​Transthoracic echocardiogram of a 24-year-old female with dyspnea on exertion and a continuous murmur heard in the left subclavicular region. (A) Parasternal short-axis view with color Doppler demonstrating high-velocity continuous flow from the descending aorta (DAo) to the main pulmonary artery (MPA). The ascending aorta (AAo) and the right pulmonary artery (RPA) are labeled. (B) Apical four-chamber view demonstrating an enlarged left ventricle (LV) due to left-to-right shunting at the great arterial level resulting in increased LV preload. The right ventricle (RV) is normal in size because the shunt does not result in increased RV preload. (C) Continuous-wave Doppler clearly demonstrates continuous left-to-right flow at a systolic velocity of 4 m/s and end diastolic velocity of 3 m/s. This patient’s noninvasive right upper extremity blood pressure at the time of the echocardiogram was 110/65 mm Hg. The estimated pulmonary artery (PA) systolic pressure is mildly elevated at 46 mm Hg (110 to 64) and the PA diastolic pressure is estimated at 29 mm Hg (65 to 36), which is moderately elevated. These findings indicate a somewhat restrictive patent ductus arteriosus that nevertheless is causing sufficient left-to-right shunting to increase the PA systolic and diastolic pressures and result in LV volume overload.

figures.caption: Fig. 17.12 ​Conical-type patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) in a 62-year-old presenting with decompensated heart failure and pulmonary edema. (A) Cineangiography, lateral projection of a mechanical contrast injection in the distal aortic arch (Ao) demonstrating a conical-type PDA with left-to-right flow to a moderately dilated main pulmonary artery (MPA). Note the size discrepancy between the enlarged aortic isthmus of the PDA and the restrictive narrowing at the MPA entry point. (B) Transthoracic echo with color Doppler, parasternal short-axis view, demonstrates diastolic flow from the descending aorta via the PDA to the pulmonary artery. The jet is directed at the pulmonary valve (PV) with resultant pulmonary valve regurgitation. (C) Subcostal view demonstrates diastolic high-velocity jet from the PDA to the PA and the PV. (D) Apical four-chamber view in systole demonstrates a dilated left ventricle (LV) with severe functional mitral regurgitation (MR). Herein one can see the long-term consequences of untreated PDA with significant left-to-right shunt and left ventricular volume overload. The patient underwent device closure of the PDA with resultant resolution of symptoms, reduction in mitral regurgitation severity, and decrease in left ventricular size.

figures.caption: Fig. 20.2 Illustration of the various sinus of Valsalva aneurysm ruptures as classified by Sakakibara and Konno.4 Type 1—The aneurysm originates from the left-side border of the right sinus of Valsalva and ruptures into the right ventricular outflow tract just below the pulmonary valve. This type of aneurysm is often coexistent with a supracristal ventricular septal defect (VSD). This is the most common of the defects and accounts for 48% of cases. Type II—The aneurysm originates from the mid part of the right sinus of Valsalva and ruptures into the right ventricle (RV); a concurrent VSD is unlikely. This defect accounts for 34% of cases. Type III—The aneurysm originates from the mid portion of the right sinus and ruptures either into the right atrium (RA) (Type IIIa) or less commonly the RV (Type IIIv) just below the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve. A VSD is rarely encountered. Type IIIa accounts for 13% of cases and type IIIv accounts for 6%. Type IV is the rarest of all and is the result of an aneurysm from the right-facing portion of the noncoronary sinus that ruptures into the RA. Ao, Aorta; LCC, left coronary cusp; NCC, noncoronary cusp; PA, pulmonary artery; RCC, right coronary cusp; TV, tricuspid valve.

figures.caption: Fig. 22.2 Illustrations of three principal varieties of tricuspid atresia without transposition of the great arteries. Anatomic arrangements proximal to the mitral valve are similar. An interatrial communication provides the right atrium (RA) with its only exit. Anatomic arrangements distal to the mitral valve vary. (A) Pulmonary atresia is represented by an intact ventricular septum. All left ventricular blood enters the aorta (Ao). The pulmonary trunk (PT) is hypoplastic. Pulmonary blood flow depends on patency of the ductus arteriosus or on systemic arterial collaterals. The left atrium (LA) and left ventricle (LV) are normal-sized. (B) Subpulmonary stenosis is represented by a restrictive ventricular septal defect between the normal-sized left ventricle (LV) and the small right ventricle (RV). The pulmonary trunk is normal or small. (C) A non-restrictive ventricular septal defect permits unobstructed blood flow into the pulmonary trunk. When pulmonary vascular resistance is low, pulmonary blood flow is increased, so the left atrium and left ventricle dilate. VSD, Ventricular septal defect.

figures.caption: Fig. 22.3 Illustration of three principal varieties of tricuspid atresia with complete transposition of the great arteries. The anatomic arrangements proximal to the mitral valve are similar. An interatrial communication provides the right atrium (RA) with its only exit. A non-restrictive ventricular septal defect permits unobstructed blood flow from the left ventricle (LV) into the transposed aorta (Ao). Anatomic arrangements distal to the mitral valve vary. (A) With atresia of the pulmonary valve, all left ventricular blood enters the Ao through the nonrestrictive ventricular septal defect. The right ventricle (RV) is well-formed, but the pulmonary trunk (PT) is hypoplastic. Pulmonary blood flow depends on patency of the ductus arteriosus or on systemic arterial collaterals. The left atrium (LA) and left ventricle (LV) are normal-sized. (B) Valvular or subvalvular pulmonary stenosis regulates pulmonary blood flow. The pulmonary trunk is well-developed. The left atrium and left ventricle remain normal-sized. (C) With no pulmonary stenosis and low pulmonary vascular resistance, pulmonary blood flow is increased, so the left atrium and left ventricle enlarge.

figures.caption: Fig. 24.5 Illustrations of the normal circulation and the distinctive circulation in transposition of the great arteries. In the normal heart, there is a single circulation in series with flow from the right ventricle (RV) into the pulmonary trunk (PT), pulmonary veins (PVs), left atrium (LA), left ventricle (LV), aorta (Ao), systemic venous bed, vena cavae, right atrium (RA), and back to the right ventricle. In complete transposition of the great arteries, there are two circulations in parallel. The systemic circulation is characterized by flow from the right ventricle into the aorta, systemic venous bed, vena cavae, right atrium, and back to the right ventricle. The pulmonary circulation is characterized by flow from left ventricle into pulmonary trunk, pulmonary veins, left atrium, and back to the left ventricle.

figures.caption: Fig. 24.25 Electrocardiogram from a deeply cyanotic 15-month-old boy with complete transposition of the great arteries, a nonrestrictive ventricular septal defect, and severe fixed subpulmonary stenosis. Peaked right atrial P waves appear in leads 2 and aVF and in lead V1. Pure right ventricular hypertrophy is reflected in marked right axis deviation, tall monophasic R waves in leads aVR and V1, and deep S waves in left precordial leads. T waves are taller in right precordial leads than in left precordial leads. Right axis deviation is moderate or absent when the left ventricle is volume overloaded in the presence of a nonrestrictive ventricular septal defect and increased pulmonary blood flow. Right axis deviation occurs when left ventricular volume overload is curtailed by pulmonary vascular disease or pulmonary stenosis (Fig. 24.27, and see Fig. 24.25). Right axis deviation is most striking when an atrial septal defect occurs with increased pulmonary blood flow, normal pulmonary artery pressure, and pure right ventricular hypertrophy (see Fig. 24.26). Left precordial R waves are small and Q waves are absent despite left ventricular volume overload (see Fig. 24.26). Pure right ventricular hypertrophy also occurs when pulmonary stenosis or a nonrestrictive ventricular septal defect with pulmonary vascular disease reduces left ventricular volume, and when a hypervolemic systemic circulation increases right ventricular volume (see Figs. 24.25 and 24.27). Biventricular hypertrophy is evidence of a nonrestrictive ventricular septal defect with low pulmonary vascular resistance and both volume and pressure overload of the left ventricle (see Fig. 24.24).80 Right precordial T waves are seldom deeply inverted, even when the systemic right ventricle is volume overloaded. Right precordial T waves are often not only positive, but tend to be distinctly taller than left precordial T waves (see Figs. 24.25 and 24.26).
